#4976. Circle’s ARC token sale lifts earnings as lower yields weigh on USDC income

Circle is looking to payments fees and future staking rewards to diversify revenue as its core stablecoin business faces pressure from lower yields and growing competition.

Circle’s expansion beyond stablecoins supplied the biggest boost to its third-quarter earnings, as the company recognized $182 million in revenue from its ARC token presale, helping offset falling income from the reserves backing its flagship stablecoin, USDC.

The company reported diluted earnings per share of $0.84, up from $0.64 a year earlier and double analysts’ expectations of $0.42. Total revenue and reserve income rose 17% to $865 million. Without the ARC token sale, however, revenue would have fallen from a year earlier.

Circle shares were down 0.84% at $74.59 at 4:05 pm UTC on Nov. 4, according to Yahoo Finance.

The results capture a transition for Circle. Its established stablecoin business earns returns on the reserves backing USDC, tying income to interest rates and the amount of the token outstanding. Its newer businesses aim to earn from the payments and financial activity those digital dollars support.

Circle launched its payments network in May 2025 to connect financial institutions settling cross-border payments with stablecoins. Arc, its blockchain for financial applications, went live on public mainnet on Sept. 16, 2026. Its native token, ARC, is intended to support network security and governance as Arc moves toward proof of stake in 2027, while transaction fees are paid in USDC.

That contribution arrived as lower reserve yields outweighed growth in USDC balances. Average circulation increased 8% year over year, but the reserve return fell 61 basis points to 3.5%. Reserve income declined 8% to $657.6 million.

Interest rates were lower than a year earlier, despite a Federal Reserve rate hike in September. The Fed raised its benchmark range by a quarter percentage point to 3.75%–4% in September, although that remained below the 4%–4.25% range set a year earlier. Circle’s reserve return also edged up from 3.48% in the second quarter, but the earnings pressure reflected the lower year-over-year yield.

USDC ended September at $73.9 billion in circulation, while its share of the stablecoin market fell 1.83 percentage points to 27%.

Competition is also expanding. Open Standard’s Open USD was live on Solana by Sept. 30, with Coinbase, Mastercard, Shopify, Stripe and Visa as founding partners. The stablecoin model distributes reserve earnings to partners after a management fee, giving businesses another option for accessing stablecoins and sharing their economics.

Related: ARK buys $17M in Coinbase, Circle shares while trimming Bullish

ARC changed Circle’s earnings picture. Excluding ARC presale revenue, total revenue and reserve income were $683 million, down roughly 8% year over year. Reported adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization rose 85% to $317 million. Without the ARC contribution, adjusted EBITDA was approximately $135 million, down 21% from $171 million a year earlier.

Circle anticipates staking rewards after Arc transitions to proof of stake, which it targets for 2027. That would create another source of revenue, although it remains dependent on the network’s development.

Circle is also beginning to charge for some payments-network activity. Chief Financial Officer Jeremy Fox-Geen said on the earnings call that the company expected material CPN revenue in 2027. CEO Jeremy Allaire described Circle’s strategy as building connected networks, with growth in stablecoins, payments and blockchain applications reinforcing one another.

“This is not just about payments, and it is not just about digital dollars. It is about multiple compounding flywheels on one platform. Every new member, every new builder, and every new asset makes the whole platform more valuable,” Allaire said.

The company is also adjusting its workforce size. The earnings disclosures included a reduction affecting approximately 5% of employees, which Circle said was intended to align its organization with its operating model and strategic priorities.

#4975. Women’s Heart Health Just Got a Major Update. Here’s What Doctors Want You to Know

This is a much-needed and overdue change.

Big news in female heart health: Four major health organizations have come together to create a shared framework and clinical guidance for women's heart health across several different life stages.

The American Heart Association, American Academy of Pediatrics, American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG), and Society for Maternal-Fetal Medicine came together to outline the “female life stage" framework to protect heart health from puberty through menopause and beyond. The framework (which essentially acts as a classification system for medical providers) was just published in the journal Circulation.

This is a big deal for many reasons, including acknowledging that female heart health and risk factors change over a woman's life. "This has been a long time coming," says Nicole Weinberg, MD, a cardiologist at Pacific Heart Institute’s Women’s Heart Center in Santa Monica, California.

According to the American Heart Association, cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of death in women, claiming more lives than breast cancer, lung cancer, and chronic lung disease combined. But only four in 10 women are aware that cardiovascular disease is the biggest threat to their health.

This new framework separates cardiovascular risk factors, along with care needs, throughout the different stages of a woman's life. Here's what you need to know.

Meet the experts: Sadiya Khan, MD, chair of the collaborative writing group and professor of Cardiovascular Epidemiology at Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine; Jennifer Haythe, MD, co-director of the Women’s Heart Center at NewYork-Presbyterian/Columbia University Irving Medical Center; and Nicole Weinberg, MD, cardiologist at Pacific Heart Institute’s Women’s Heart Center in Santa Monica, California

The Female Life Stage framework is defined by hormone changes specific to girls and women at different stages of life, hence the name. The framework also recognizes pregnancy as an event that can impact cardiovascular health at any or several life stages. Here's a breakdown of each:

Adopting this new way of classifying female life stages “offers a transformative opportunity to equitably improve cardiovascular health for all girls and women," the researchers wrote in the review article.

This has never been done before. “For the first time, four major medical groups agree that a woman’s heart health is shaped by every stage of her life, from her first period to menopause," says Jennifer Haythe, MD, co-director of the Women’s Heart Center at NewYork-Presbyterian/Columbia University Irving Medical Center.

This helps address the "fragmentation of care" that can happen between ob-gyns, cardiologists, and other specialists who care for women, says Sadiya Khan, MD, chair of the collaborative writing group and professor of Cardiovascular Epidemiology at Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine. "We're all speaking different languages and we're all speaking different levels of care, yet they're all connected," she says.

The framework is a "shared playbook" that doctors from different specialties can use to guide patient care, along with a language that's understandable and easy to communicate for everyone, Dr. Khan says. "It's really connecting those aspects of health that we think are disconnected," she says.

This new system helps to bridge the gap between viewing cardiovascular care as something completely separate from women's health. "This is meant to reframe cardiovascular health as part of a woman's care," says Dr. Khan. "Any of these things may influence the other."

Weinberg says the framework will create "a more unified view" of women's health. "By creating a road map that is shared by pediatricians, cardiologists, ob-gyns, and maternal-fetal medicine doctors, things like PMOS, irregular periods, pregnancy complications, and metabolic shifts in perimenopause will be treated as real heart health signals, so early warning signs aren’t missed," Haythe says.

Carina Hsieh, MPH, is the deputy features editor of Women’s Health. She has more than a decade’s worth of experience working in media and has covered everything from beauty, fashion, travel, lifestyle, pets, to health.

She began her career as an intern in the fashion closet at Cosmopolitan where she worked her way up to Senior Sex & Relationships Editor. While covering women’s health there, she discovered her passion for health service journalism and took a break to get her Masters in Public Health. Post-grad school, she worked as a freelance writer and as The Daily Beast’s first Beauty, Health, and Wellness Reporter.

Carina is an alum of the Fashion Institute of Technology and the Yale School of Public Health. She and her French Bulldog, Bao Bao, split their time between Brooklyn and Connecticut. She enjoys reformer Pilates, (slow) running, and smelling the fancy toiletries in boutique fitness class locker rooms.

#4974. Riot shares surge on $28B AI lease as Hut 8 sinks on revenue miss

Bitcoin miner Riot sold BTC to finance its AI expansion, while Hut 8 reported falling revenue and rising costs before its major data center leases generate income.

Shares of Bitcoin miner Riot Platforms surged more than 13% Wednesday after the company announced a $28 billion AI data center lease, its largest agreement to date as it accelerates its expansion into artificial intelligence infrastructure.

The 15-year agreement covers 910 megawatts at its Corsicana, Texas, facility, bringing its total future contracted data center revenue to approximately $38 billion across three leases signed this year. The agreement represents a major step in Riot’s AI infrastructure strategy as it moves away from relying primarily on Bitcoin mining revenue.

“A year ago, our cash flow depended on the price of Bitcoin, and now, at full deployment of currently executed deals, nearly all of our expected cash flow will be generated from long-term leases with leading players in the AI ecosystem,” CEO Jason Les said during Wednesday’s earnings call.

According to Riot’s third-quarter earnings release, Riot will provide land and power infrastructure originally developed for Bitcoin mining, while the AI tenant, identified as Anthropic in the company’s quarterly filing, will own and operate the computing equipment and cover operating expenses.

Riot estimates the project’s total capital costs at $5.5 billion, financed primarily through debt backed by lease payments, although financing has not yet been secured. The first phase is expected to be delivered in September 2027, with rental payments beginning within 60 days of delivery.

Riot also reported third-quarter revenue of $181.4 million, up just 1% year over year, and sold 10,599 BTC during the quarter to help finance its data center expansion. During Wednesday’s earnings call, CEO Jason Les said Bitcoin mining at Corsicana could begin winding down in summer 2027.

Related: Bitcoin miners face widening AI financing costs as lenders scrutinize deals

Meanwhile, shares of fellow Bitcoin miner Hut 8 plunged more than 22% at one point on Wednesday after the company reported weaker-than-expected quarterly revenue amid its transition toward AI infrastructure.

Third-quarter revenue fell 15% to $71.1 million, missing analysts’ estimates of $75.8 million, according to MarketBeat data. During Wednesday’s earnings call, CFO Sean Glennan attributed the decline partly to asset sales and lower revenue per Bitcoin mined, while cash administrative expenses also rose year over year.

“The legacy revenue base is no longer the main growth driver, while the larger contracted infrastructure revenues remain tied to delivery milestones,” Glennan said.

CEO Asher Genoot also pointed to the complexity and expense of traditional AI data center construction as the company looks to develop projects on a larger scale.

“Many of today’s data centers resemble NASA rocket programs—remarkable engineering, but complex, expensive, and slow to deliver,” Genoot said.

According to the company’s third-quarter earnings presentation, Hut 8 has already secured $7.5 billion in project bonds to fully finance two major AI data center developments, although neither has begun generating lease revenue.

#4972. Trump-linked tokens lead crypto losses after Democrats sweep in the US midterms

The official Trump and World Liberty Financial tokens were the two biggest losers among the top 100 cryptocurrencies on Wednesday, even as Bitcoin and Ether rallied.

Two crypto tokens linked to US President Donald Trump led losses among the top 100 digital assets on Wednesday following the US midterm elections, raising questions about their future as the broader crypto market rallied.

Official Trump (TRUMP) fell 17% over 24 hours to $1.33, while World Liberty Financial (WLFI) dropped over 7% to $0.047, according to CoinMarketCap data from around 5:32 pm UTC. TRUMP is the president’s official memecoin, launched in January 2025, while WLFI is the governance token of World Liberty Financial, a Trump family-backed decentralized finance (DeFi) project launched in 2024.

The declines followed a wave of Democratic victories, including surprise wins in Texas, in Tuesday’s midterm elections, with the party winning control of both the House and Senate from Republicans.

The results could not only make it harder for Trump to push forward his crypto plans but also bring more scrutiny to his family’s crypto businesses. Analysts say the losses also raise questions about whether political sentiment alone can fuel demand for Trump-linked tokens.

Bitcoin (BTC) rose more than 4% over 24 hours to around $80,500, while Ether (ETH) climbed 6% to $2,433, according to CoinMarketCap data. Other major cryptocurrencies also posted gains, with BNB rising 3%, XRP climbing 2.6% and Solana (SOL) gaining 2.5%. The overall crypto market rose 3.4% to $2.69 trillion.

Meanwhile, the losses extended to other Trump family-linked tokens, such as the MELANIA memecoin, associated with First Lady Melania Trump. MELANIA dropped nearly 13% over 24 hours to around $0.066.

A separate token named after Vice President JD Vance (VANCE) also dropped nearly 12%, although it has no confirmed official connection to the vice president.

The losses were further reflected across the broader political memecoin market, with the sector’s total market capitalization falling more than 16% on the day to $477 million. Trading volume jumped 123% to $437 million, per CoinMarketCap data.

Related: US midterm elections 2026 as it happened: Democrats win control of Congress

Benjamin Sarquis Peillard, founder and CEO of Cap, a DeFi platform focused on stablecoin yields, told Cointelegraph that investors appear to be treating politically linked tokens differently from other cryptocurrencies.

“Bitcoin and other established assets respond to a combination of liquidity, institutional flows and macroeconomic conditions, while politically linked tokens can be more sensitive to shifts in expectations around Washington,” he said. “Even as the broader market recovers, those tokens may face selling pressure if investors begin reassessing their risk exposure.”

And while the selloff could be indicative of a short-term reaction to the election results, Peillard said the “longer-term question is what supports demand for these tokens beyond their association with a political figure.”

Beyond the market reaction, the election results also raise questions about the future of US crypto legislation, including the currently stalled Digital Asset Market Clarity Act, commonly referred to as the CLARITY Act.

The bill, which aims to establish a regulatory framework for digital assets, failed to advance in the Senate earlier this year after falling short of the 60 votes required. Democrats were pushing for stronger ethical provisions and safeguards against conflicts of interest involving Trump’s crypto ventures — four Republicans also opposed advancing the legislation.

“The midterm results introduce a new layer of regulatory uncertainty, particularly around the pace and direction of digital asset legislation,” Peillard said. “For politically linked tokens, that uncertainty can have a more immediate impact because investor sentiment is partly tied to expectations around the political environment.”

While the crypto sector continues to have support — and opposition — from lawmakers in both parties, it remains to be seen how the election results will affect crypto legislation.

Peillard said that for the broader industry, the “more important question is whether Congress can establish a durable regulatory framework that provides clarity regardless of which party holds power.”

Her secret weapon to a successful training block? A lot of naps and even more tea.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

Speaking from personal experience, the closer you get to marathon day, the louder the worries become. Can I really make it to the start line when I’m so sore and tired all the time? Are my long runs and weekly mileage on par with everyone else’s? Do I even want to be doing this anymore? That is, unless you’re the reigning champion, Hellen Obiri.

This weekend, she’ll be making her return to the New York City Marathon—which she won last year in a course record of 2 hours, 19 minutes, 51 seconds. When I chatted with the On athlete a few weeks out from the race, she had just wrapped up a morning session of 12.4 miles and still had another five on deck later that day. It seems like a lot, but “the evening session is always very easy,” she assured me.

Obiri, 36, has won four marathons (NYC and Boston, two times each), and though she knows everyone will be watching to see if she’ll do it again, she doesn’t seem affected by the pressure. “When you're the reigning champion, everybody's looking at you and wondering what you can do,” she says. “You have that pressure of, ‘How can I win back to back?’”

But Obiri knows that in a marathon, anything can happen. It’s a long distance, and she’s competing against the best of the best—so she’s not counting a single person out. “For me, [the key] is to keep training well, and to keep that in my mind: I'm the defending champion,” Obiri says. “The most important thing is to stay safe and to stay healthy, and then everything's possible.”

Here’s what she’s doing to prepare for race day—and her advice to those heading to a starting line soon.

Because, well, it worked so well in 2025. “Sometimes we do study who is in the race,” she admits, though she didn’t name drop any one contender she has her eye on this year.

Each week, she logs over 100 miles, and gives herself two to three days to recover after a long run or speed session. (Recovery days still often consist of easy miles, though.) Her longest run heading into November 1? Twenty-four miles. Even the best of the best don’t run the full distance until race day.

She also preps—both physically and mentally—for pushing through particularly hard moments. Will she still have enough in the tank to keep pushing the pace with her speedy competitors come mile 20? What about in those last 100 meters if she needs to dig deep for a sprint finish?

It’s her second year working with On Athletic Club coach Laura Thweatt, who also boasts an impressive history with the NYC Marathon, placing eighth in 2021. Having a coach who has also raced New York has made a huge difference, Obiri says, because she knows what it’s like to train for this specific race and also what it takes to do well. Plus, Thweatt is able to join her on runs (though she won’t be running the race herself). “She’s my training partner,” Obiri says.

Thweatt is also Obiri’s first-ever female coach, and that’s not to be underestimated, either. “To have a female coach, you can't hide something from her,” Obiri says. “She already knows everything, what you're going through in your mind, in your body.”

Beyond running, Obiri does strength work three times per week, focusing on lower-body muscles like her calves and glutes, but surprisingly, she’s pretty focused on her arms, too. At her level, everything counts, including how strong your arms are when you’re swinging them during a race—an area that needs some improvement, she says.

She naps. Often. After her morning session, Obiri takes a snooze. Then, she heads to lunch. After lunch? She’s napping again. “I sleep a lot,” she says. Obiri estimates that she spends anywhere from five to six hours a day napping.

For Obiri, the basics—sleeping, eating, and hydrating—are the most important things for feeling her best. And when it comes to hydration, Obiri’s not getting caught up in the electrolyte craze or downing gallons of water. Instead, she relies on tea as her main source for fluids. She drinks all different kinds, but will make it in a big batch, complete with milk and three spoonfuls of sugar per cup.

“I’m addicted to tea with sugar,” she says. She has about seven cups per day, including before a run. It’s an easy way to get some extra carbs in, for sure. Along with her tea, before her 6:45 a.m. run, Obiri will have two slices of bread and a banana. “I can’t go on my runs with an empty stomach,” she says.

“The most important thing is to listen to your body,” she says. You might be feeling the excitement right off the bat or trying to keep up with the crowd, but remember to pay attention to how you feel and not go too hard too soon. “Don't go crazy because it's a marathon—it's a long journey—and needs patience,” she says. Make sure you’re keeping on top of fluids and fuel, too.

At this point, you may be deep into training and feeling drained—that’s completely normal, but does require a mindset shift. When Obiri is lacking motivation, she just tells herself she has to do it, or at least start it. “If I start, I will finish it,” she says. And, when a run gets hard? No matter how far she is from the end, she tells herself, “I’m almost there.”

It’s possible your For You Page (like mine) is filled with people freaking out about where they’re at in training—and it can be pretty easy to compare yourself to them. Maybe you have friends crushing long runs on Strava and are starting to wonder if it says anything about your progress.

Whatever it is, stay focused on your own program. “Everybody trains differently, so just know you have trained well and focus on your body, and trust me, you’ll be at the finish line and run well,” Obiri says.

Ultimately, your marathon is about you and what you did to get there. “Trust yourself, trust what you have been training for, and be ready to do what you have been training for six months or longer,” Obiri says.

She reports, writes, and edits content ranging from service stories to in-depth features and awards packages across all verticals, including health, fitness, sports, and beauty. While at WH, she’s traveled to Paris, France to watch Faith Kipyegon attempt a sub-4-minute mile and covered major races like Ultra Trail du Mont Blanc in Chamonix. Olivia is a RRCA-certified running coach who is especially passionate about helping people start their running journey and is training for her second marathon. Her works also appears in New York Magazine’s The Cut, PS (formerly Popsugar), and Salon, where she also did on-camera interviews with celebrity guests.

#4970. How Aussie Bitcoiners can avoid 2027’s shock CGT hike

From setting up an SMSF or a company, to just leaving the country entirely, here are some strategies Australian Bitcoiners can employ to deal with 2027’s massive CGT hike.

The Australian government’s decision to scrap the 50% capital gains discount for all investments in the May budget came as a big shock for crypto owners. The new scheme effectively doubles the taxable component of a gain, minus a small discount for inflation.

But there are legal ways to minimize the amount of CGT you’ll have to pay — if you start prepping now.

Some Aussie crypto holders are taking drastic measures — like Finder founder and crypto king Fred Schebesta who is relocating to Singapore which offers 0% CGT, stating the tax changes were a “killer blow.”But there are less dramatic methods to reduce your CGT bills including setting up a self managed super fund (SMSF), a company to trade crypto at the company tax rate, or to just cross your fingers and hope the opposition will reverse the changes after the next election.

Since 1999, Aussie asset owners have only paid tax on half of their capital gain. From July 1, 2027 they’ll pay their full income tax rate — which means 30% CGT if your income and gains are between A$45,000 and $135,000, 37% for the portion between $135,000 and $190,000 and 47% above that. (All figures in this story are in Aussie dollars)

Adding insult to injury, low-income earners who aren’t on welfare like students and retirees will pay a minimum 30% CGT rate no matter how little the gain.

The only discount now available accounts for the effect of inflation on your cost basis. So if you buy a house for $1 million in 2027 and sell it for $1.5 million after 10 years, with inflation at 3%, you won’t have to pay tax on the $344,000 or so attributed to inflation.

“The challenge for cryptocurrency is that the CGT changes, indexation really helps slower growing assets not fast ones,” explains Andrea Yuen, Swyftx CEO.

So if you bought Bitcoin for $10,000 and sell it ten years later for $100,000, the inflation discount is only around $3,439. Under the old system you would pay tax on $45,000 of gains. Under the new system you’ll pay tax on $86,561 of gains.

Stockspot analyst Chris Bryki compared how ten different asset classes would fare under the new rules. “Crypto sits at the bottom because almost its entire return comes from capital growth,” he wrote in The Australian newspaper.

Here are a few different strategies to help crypto holders deal with the changes, ranging from little to no effort, to restructuring your entire life.

Any gain you’ve made before July 1 2027 will be taxed under the existing 50% discount scheme. So your best bet is to hope a raging bull market pushes the value of your portfolio as high as possible before that date.You should faithfully record the value of every crypto asset you have that day, as any gain from that value will be taxed at the higher rate.

Ben Simpson, founder of crypto advisory service Collective Shift, says Bitcoin’s performance since mid-year in a challenging macro environment bodes well for further gains before July.

But Simpson (who points out he’s not a financial advisor) adds, “I probably wouldn’t be betting the farm on the fact that we’re gonna have a huge bull run”

Yuen notes that prices aren’t within your control.  “A strategy isn’t a strategy if you’re just sort of hoping,” she says.

Both the official opposition The Coalition, and the insurgent opposition One Nation, have promised to reverse the changes. Crypto voters who feel strongly enough about this single issue, could vote for a change in government.However, the ruling ALP holds 94 out of 150 seats in the House of Representatives and will be difficult to dislodge from office. If the government does change — and the legislation can pass the Senate in time — it’s technically possible the changes could be reversed before anyone has to file taxes from July 1 2028.

But it’s probably more likely that any change to the system would occur after that date. Adrian Forza, director of Crypto Tax Australia, says this would make calculating gains very difficult.

Australian retirement funds are called superannuation funds, and once you are over 60 you can access your investments tax-free — even as they keep growing.Unfortunately none of the retail super funds allow clients to invest in crypto, so if you want to protect your crypto gains using this method, you’d have to set up an SMSF. About a third of Simpson’s high net worth clients invest in crypto via SMSFs.  “Buying Bitcoin and accumulating it there is a super solid idea,” he says, although he cautions against adding many altcoins. “You’re risking your retirement, which is an ultra long-term hold, on short-term altcoins,” he says.

Australian super fund AMP has invested in Bitcoin — but doesn’t allow its clients to do so.

The big drawback with SMSFs — explains the 27-year-old founder — is that younger crypto investors can’t access the money for decades.

Realistically then, it’s a strategy more suited to wealthier investors aged over 50, who have a shorter period to wait.

Related: Older investors are risking everything for a crypto-funded retirement

The government has also made running an SMSF a pain in the backside, with lots of compliance paperwork and audits, as well as a bunch of unavoidable fees that make it prohibitive for smaller balances. Annual costs typically range between $2,000 and $4,000, although online providers like Stake can reduce total annual costs to around $1,330, as long as you only buy Bitcoin or Ether ETFs.

You also have to sell any crypto and pay tax on it before you can rebuy it with your SMSF, and there are annual contribution limits to factor in, although Forza says you should be able to get almost $400,000 in there with a bit of creativity.

Keep an eye out in December for a detailed report on how to set up a crypto SMSF.

A strategy some billionaires employ to avoid paying tax is by borrowing against their assets, as repaying the loan often works out cheaper than paying tax on a sale.

Bitcoiners can now access a range of lenders, including BlockEarner, Vield and Swyftx, that let you employ a similar strategy by borrowing against your BTC as collateral.

“We like to bring that strategy to the masses, not just to billionaires,” laughs Yuen.

But it can be risky if you don’t have a billionaire’s deep pockets. Borrowers face high interest rates, relatively short loan periods (typically 12 months), and risk losing their Bitcoin if the market moves against them. You can’t borrow against the full value either — Swyftx has a loan-to-value ratio around 40%.”If your collateral drops below a certain amount, there will be a margin call,” she says.  “I would say it’s a bet on a price going up. I think you have to have a view that crypto will go up — or at least not go down so that you get margin-called... Otherwise, a crypto-backed loan wouldn’t make sense for you.”

Simpson doesn’t recommend this strategy due to the risks, but says it can pay off for some people. For example if you borrow at 10% interest, and Bitcoin compounds by 33% a year (as it has done in the past) you’d end up much better off than paying CGT.

But he warns it’s a leveraged bet that is best suited to sophisticated investors.

Bitcoin is down 28% over the past year, so anyone borrowing a year ago would have faced margin calls and possible liquidation as well as interest costs.

Borrowing against Bitcoin for a house deposit has become a more popular strategy. (BlockEarner)

Forza cautions that borrowing crypto can also be a CGT event in some circumstances, such as borrowing in DeFi. If you deposit ETH to Aave, it gets automatically swapped to WETH which  is a taxable event, and when you withdraw the ETH it’s another taxable event.

Borrowing from centralized lenders like BlockEarner or Swyftx is currently a grey area, and the ATO has not clarified if it’s a taxable event.”If you’re talking about [borrowing] ten grand fine. But if you’ve got three to five Bitcoin, I wouldn’t risk it because if it goes against you then you’re going to be paying tax.””Vield is the only one in Australia that’s got a private ruling that says their product is not a taxable event. No one else has got one.”Swftxy confirmed it has not got a private ruling and said clients should seek tax advice, while BlockEarner did not respond to a request for comment.

In part two of our Aussie CGT special, coming later this week, we’ll bring you the final four strategies to minimize your crypto tax bills, including setting up a company or leaving the country entirely.

#4962. Crypto PACs eye 2028 ‘new map’ as Democrats take Congress

Crypto super PACs spent more than $176 million on the midterms, but the Democratic sweep raises the prospect of tougher industry scrutiny.

Two years after crypto money helped drive Sherrod Brown out of the Senate, roughly $64 million couldn’t keep him from returning.

Brown’s victory over Republican Jon Husted in Ohio delivered the industry its biggest electoral loss of the 2026 midterms as Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress. The sweep also puts Sen. Elizabeth Warren, one of crypto’s fiercest critics, in line to chair the Senate Banking Committee.

Crypto super PACs spent about $176 million across 100 seats during the election cycle, including primaries, according to Reuters, up from more than $130 million in 2024. Fairshake and its affiliated PACs accounted for $154.5 million across 89 races.

“The next Congress will bring a fundamentally different environment for crypto in Washington, and the industry should expect significantly more scrutiny,” Kyle Bligen, executive director at the Decentralization Research Center, told Cointelegraph.

Fairshake, meanwhile, is left with more than $67 million heading to the 2028 elections. “Newly elected and current members will have a choice: protect consumers and American jobs or fight progress,” spokesperson Geoff Vetter told Cointelegraph in an email. “We will be watching and ‘28 is a new map.”

Ohio was the industry’s biggest bet as crypto PACs put more than $64 million into keeping Senator Jon Husted in office. His opponent, former Sen. Sherrod Brown, won the special election to complete former Sen. JD Vance’s term, which ends in January 2029. He could seek a senior role on the Senate Agriculture Committee, which oversees the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC).

Brown’s comeback came two years after crypto’s biggest win in 2024, when Fairshake spent $40 million to help Bernie Moreno unseat him in Ohio’s other Senate seat. Some industry leaders treated that result as a warning to Congress. Gemini exchange co-founder Cameron Winklevoss declared on X: “This is what happens when you mess with the crypto army”.

This year, crypto spending was part of a much larger flood of outside money. Independent expenditures in the race topped $350 million, while Brown turned the crypto spending into a campaign theme, writing “I’ll be damned if crypto billionaires decide this race,” in a campaign message.

The loss in Ohio may weaken the perception that defying crypto PACs carries an electoral cost in Washington. Before the vote, a Republican crypto lobbyist told Politico that a Brown win would “neuter Fairshake’s perceived Sword of Damocles.”

Nebraska, meanwhile, offered crypto PACs a significant win, with Sen. Pete Ricketts retaining his seat after Fairshake affiliate Defend American Jobs spent $13.5 million opposing independent challenger Dan Osborn.

“As the biggest spender in the Nebraska Senate race, we’re proud to have helped Sen. Ricketts weather the waves of a hard-fought cycle,” wrote Vetter. “Fairshake played a meaningful role in winning competitive races across the country in 2026 and we will do it again in 2028.” The PAC’s other Senate wins came in Republican strongholds, including Barry Moore in Alabama and Andy Barr in Kentucky.

Other spending failed to deliver the intended results, both in primaries and in November. The Fairshake network’s roughly $10 million spent opposing Juliana Stratton in the Illinois Democratic primary failed to block her nomination. She later won the Senate seat. In Massachusetts, John Deaton lost despite roughly $700,000 in spending by crypto-backed Commonwealth Unity Fund to help elect him. Ken Paxton, who received crypto PAC backing in his successful Texas Republican runoff against John Cornyn, went on to lose to James Talarico.

The House brought another setback when digital assets subcommittee chair Bryan Steil lost to Democrat Mitchell Berman despite $1.9 million in crypto PAC funding.

The shift in congressional control could slow crypto legislation, but BitGo CEO and co-founder Mike Belshe said the election results would not alter the industry’s trajectory. “Crypto has continued to move forward under different administrations and different political majorities. The GENIUS Act is now law, stablecoin rules are moving ahead, and regulators are continuing to work on tokenization and digital asset markets.”Democratic victories could also bring crypto supporters into the Senate. Advocacy group Stand With Crypto counted 19 winning Senate candidates it classified as pro-crypto and eight as anti-crypto, with 33 of the 35 Senate races called as of 9:45 p.m. UTC on Nov. 4.

Despite the crypto PAC spending against him in Texas, Talarico voted for the Texas Bitcoin reserve as a state lawmaker and is rated by the group as strongly supportive of crypto.

For industry advocates, the next challenge is building relationships with incoming lawmakers. Jessica Martinez, US policy director at Fireblocks, told Cointelegraph that many newly elected members had limited records on crypto, making “educating members early” key to shaping the Democratic policy agenda.

#4959. Where to Buy Vintage Lamps (2026): 1stDibs, Etsy, and More

Listen—we’ve all fallen prey to the sort of lighting lethargy that keeps our hastily-purchased mass market table lamps on our bedside. A fluorescent task lamp might still hover over the couch, a garish flush mount shedding its harsh light. So why a vintage lamp? Because it indicates you thought about your lighting instead of going the route of a last-minute, add-to-cart impulse buy. This was deliberately searched and purchased. This was a choice made with historical design context in mind, whether it’s midcentury modern, Art Deco, or Hollywood Regency. A carefully considered piece of lighting shows your home decor chops—you’ve gone above and beyond the look of the room to consider the vibe of the room. A magnificent vintage piece communicates all that. We rounded up a few retailer options to find just the thing you need for a living room revamp, a ceiling light overhaul, or a lampshade upgrade.

We pull from 1stDibs regularly when shopping out our various home tours, where we can find the iconic works sprinkled throughout the homes of celebrities, designers, and celebrity designers. A Charlotte Perriand sconce indicates at least one substantial coffee book on the oeuvre of Le Corbusier is nearby, and a reissue of the 1960’s Gelato lamp by Italian designer Carlo Nason’s are just the tip of the iceberg. In other words: Design dorks will delight in this catalog of artifacts and iconic pieces.

Etsy is a go-to when you’re searching for a vibe rather than a specific model or designer. Try keyword searching for terms like “Art Deco” or “ginger jar lamp” and a trove of collectibles, like thrift-store-friendly finds and veritable antique gems, will surface in search. The online marketplace’s vast web of sellers means a library of vintage lighting that spans centuries and styles, often times for less than what you’d find at places like 1st Dibs and Chairish since sellers choose what they price for shipping. Contributor Lori Keong has had good luck buying pieces there from across the pond in the UK and even further afield in Slovenia, with lots of vintage sellers from the states like Philly’s Betsu and Chicago’s Spears Furnishings selling their wares on Etsy as well.

eBay brought me such things as this vintage Tarogo frog made from Ichiban rice paper that I passed up in a thrift store in Maine and thought about for months before it surfaced on the secondhand retailer. Now he sits proudly on an armoire overlooking my dining room. Which is to say: Every vintage table lamp that’s ever existed is somewhere in their backlog. Chinoiserie, vintage Noguchi lamps, kitschy conch shell lamps, Tiffany glass shades, the OG Pixar lamp—it’s all there.

Design Within Reach regularly re-issues iconic models in collaboration with the original manufacturers, giving second life to pieces like Verner Panton’s Panthella (1971), Herman Miller’s 1952 Cigar Lotus floor lamp, Greta Grossman’s 1947 Gräshoppa, and the Space Age-y Nessino table lamp which debuted in 1967, to name a few.

Rejuvenation’s vintage collection is part of a larger initiative to prevent waste. The brand’s Portland-based restoration studio team finds and restores over 3,000 antiques around the world every year to help keep them out of landfills. While the vintage pieces are one-of-a-kind finds, a large selection mirrors Rejuvenation’s midcentury modern-inspired offerings, like 20th-century brass lamps and designs with floral and gilt detailing.

Abask has some of the most beautiful antique Murano glassware lamps we’ve seen to date. Case in point: Albano Poli’s stained glass creation pictured below. The artist got his claim to fame for collaging colored glass across geometric lighting fixtures. Modern glass lamps like this one are easy to come by across Abask’s collections, as well as minimalist metal lamps and hand-painted ceramic lamps, if those better suit your style.

#4958. BitMart founder says security team ‘severely understaffed’ after new hack

The crypto exchange’s founder warned of security staffing shortages amid restructuring as analysts flagged suspicious transfers potentially linked to the Mercado Bitcoin hack.

Cryptocurrency exchange BitMart is operating with an understaffed security team following restructuring, its founder said Wednesday, after confirming a new hack that may be linked to the recent attack on Brazil’s exchange Mercado Bitcoin.

In a post on X, BitMart founder Sheldon Xia said threats against employees and alleged retaliation by former staff had complicated efforts to retain technical personnel.

“It took considerable effort and individual conversations to persuade some key technical staff to remain and maintain our core systems,” Xia wrote. “However, we continue to face numerous attacks. Our security team is currently severely understaffed, but we are still doing everything we can to safeguard data and assets.”

Xia described the amount involved in Monday’s hack as small but did not disclose a figure. Blockchain analytics firm Bitquery identified approximately $391,000 in suspicious transfers from wallets mostly associated with BitMart across three blockchains, according to a Wednesday investigation.

Bitquery traced the funds to a wallet also implicated in the more than $46 million Mercado Bitcoin hack on Monday, Nov. 2, supporting Xia’s preliminary suspicion of a possible connection between the incidents.

Related: North Korea denies role in $6.3B Binance hack, points finger at US

The latest breach comes amid months of uncertainty over BitMart’s future. The exchange announced in July that it would end trading on Aug. 26 and cease operations in January 2027. Following the announcement, users reported delayed withdrawals and frozen accounts, raising concerns about access to their funds.

In August, BitMart’s Chinese-language X account alleged that employees had gone unpaid and demanded answers about customer funds. The founder dismissed the allegations as fabricated, though it remained unclear who controlled the account at the time.

In a restructuring proposal published Monday, the exchange outlined three potential recovery options for users, including liquid asset distributions and recovery-linked tokens, with plans to seek court approval in December or January.

Cointelegraph contacted BitMart for details about the restructuring, security staffing and latest breach but had not received a response by publication.

Separately, a crypto crime-fighting alliance formed by Tron, Tether and TRM Labs has dissolved amid a wave of major industry hacks, Bloomberg reported Wednesday.

The T3 Financial Crime Unit, launched in September 2024 and later joined by Binance, struggled with slow responses and poor coordination, Bloomberg reported, citing people familiar with the matter. One source said the group disbanded in late August.

In May, T3 said it had helped freeze more than $450 million in assets linked to suspected criminal activity since its launch in 2024.

The group’s dissolution comes amid a wave of major crypto hacks, including last week’s $6.3 billion Binance breach, the largest cryptocurrency theft on record.

#4956. She Had a Bad Day and Consulted a Psychic. It Destroyed Her Life.

Intuitive practices have brought comfort to millions—but for some, it has opened the door to predators who weaponize belief, hope, and the search for healing.

IN EARLY 2024, a young Los Angeles musician who was down on her luck met with the FBI. She had a story that, at first, seemed unbelievable.

Nine months earlier, her career faltering and her morale low, she was approached one night by a psychic. The psychic said she could see that something was bothering her and offered to do a palm reading. The reading showed spiritual blockages hanging over the musician’s life, and the psychic said they would need to work together closely to clear them.

The musician gave the psychic thousands of dollars, the amounts increasing over time, and even bought cars for her and her family. At the psychic’s instruction, the musician lied to her own family, extracting what she could from them. When that wasn’t enough, the psychic put her to work. But now, confused and desperate, and overwhelmed by how she had even ended up in this situation in the first place, the musician needed to tell someone what had happened to her.

When the FBI ran the psychic’s name in their system, they discovered a familiar narrative of victimization had played out at least once before. Gina Rita Russell—psychic hustler, skilled manipulator, and pill-popping madame—was already on the FBI’s radar. And the story that put her there, beginning more than a decade earlier, was wilder than anyone could have imagined.

ONE NIGHT IN the fall of 2009, Jill Smith* was walking home through the streets of New York City, her self-esteem at an all-time low. Smith, 24, had just lost her job and gone through a devastating breakup. She felt vulnerable and rudderless, unable to launch her adult life. She’d been crying herself to sleep every night. When she passed a psychic storefront in the West Village, Gina Rita Russell was sitting outside at a small table. “Come for a reading,” Russell called out warmly. Smith declined politely, but Russell was persistent. So Smith took a seat and handed over $40.

Russell described herself as a “spiritual guider.” She peered into Smith’s palm, holding it in her own plump hands, and said she could see why Smith’s life was uncomfortably stalled. Even worse, she could see more bad things down the road. Smith needed Russell’s help, and fast. They would have to do “the work” to clear the mystical clouds hanging over Smith’s future, “driving the demons out” together. For the first time in a while, Smith’s despair lightened. She felt relieved that Russell wanted to help her.

What began as a cautious friendship at a rough time in a young woman’s life soon morphed into a nightmare. Over the next eight years, Russell would push Smith to abandon relationships, walk away from her budding career, and engage in degrading acts to clear what she was told was a malignant hex. And then, when the spell was finally broken, Smith would face a new uphill battle common to victims of trafficking: trying to persuade the courts that she wasn’t a coconspirator but a victim of forces that even she struggled to explain.

GROWING INTEREST IN “spiritual wellness” is driving the purchase of shiny little crystals and the borrowing of chants from Eastern traditions, plus plenty of yoga-and-gratitude retreats in places all over the world. But as part of this trend, some women are also leaning on psychics and other intuitive practitioners.

According to recent Pew research, 30 percent of Americans now consult astrology, tarot cards, or fortune tellers at least once a year. For women under 50, 43 percent “believe in astrology,” while only 27 percent of women 50 and over do. Eight percent of women say they rely at least a little on astrology, tarot cards, or fortune tellers to make big life decisions. Psychics are now ubiquitous, from small storefronts in one-stoplight towns to psychic influencers on Instagram with hundreds of thousands of followers. In November, Oprah had a psychic medium on her podcast discussing how to communicate with dead relatives. It can all be in good fun and perhaps even offer a bit of clarity. But at other times, it can veer into a form of exploitation.

In Jenkintown, Pennsylvania, a man-woman team with multiple fortune-telling charges against them allegedly fleeced a woman of more than $600,000, convincing her that they needed the money to lift a curse (their court cases are pending). A mother and daughter in Australia were recently arrested for allegedly running a $46 million psychic scam in which they told victims to sign over loans so they could use their powers to make the victims rich. And a woman in Toronto was allegedly scammed out of almost $8,000 by a Texas psychic she met on TikTok following the death of her stepfather. She was eager for guidance, and the cost of readings escalated quickly. “She would say I need more money to get rid of all this negativity—like, I need to fix you,” the woman said in describing the psychic to a reporter.

In some rare cases, exploitation can go far beyond theft, forcing victims into previously unimaginable acts. These relationships often start with grooming—the victim being offered kindness and attention—and then quickly shift into one-sided demands. The dynamics of control and manipulation depend on a power imbalance, and when the potential perpetrator is in a nontraditional form of authority with fewer guardrails in place, such as psychics and gurus, there may be a higher risk factor. Soon, victims may find themselves isolated, their resources depleted and their sense of reality in serious question.

“The exploiter is very intentional and thoughtful about identifying what that person needs the most and offering it to them, training them to trust them, to believe in them,” says Korin Hoffman Arkin, director of survivor care and engagement for Polaris, a national anti-trafficking organization. “So then when [an exploiter] starts asking for things that are maybe not so wonderful, it’s confusing. It starts out small and starts to build.”

While these stories might seem far-fetched, experts say that anyone can succumb to sophisticated manipulation tactics and the power of a trauma bond between victims and their tormentors. A false sense of security, of believing that one is invulnerable, creates its own risks, explains Laura Dryjanska, an associate professor at Rosemead School of Psychology of Biola University. “All of a sudden, you’re in much more danger because you’re not street smart,” she says. “People don’t realize that those psychological bonds can be much stronger than someone physically chained to a bed.”

SMITH WASN’T SOMEONE who seemed poised to veer off the tracks. She had been raised by supportive parents in upper-middle-class comfort in Long Island, New York, and earned a 3.49 GPA in theater production and design at Ithaca College. She didn’t smoke and only drank occasionally; her friends in college called her “Mom” because, mature beyond her years, she took care of everyone. After graduating from college in 2006, Smith looked for work as a designer, stylist, and wardrobe supervisor. She was thrilled when she landed a job on the soap opera Guiding Light. Smith, who has long chestnut hair and a toothy smile, was finding her feet in the big city, dealing with the exhilarating victories and demoralizing setbacks of early adulthood, impatient to live up to her promise. And then she met Russell.

Russell was just 24 when she beckoned Smith, and her background couldn’t have been more different. Her parents were Roma, a traditionally nomadic ethnic group from Eastern Europe, and she never attended school and is functionally illiterate. (As an adult, she would communicate by text using audio commands.) According to Russell, she and her siblings were forced at a young age by their parents, who were frequently violent, to support the family by selling trinkets on the streets and performing bogus psychic readings. By 15, already getting drunk and smoking marijuana, she says she was forced by her father into an informal marriage with her third cousin, Robert. Russell gave birth to the first of their four children at 16—though she eventually lost custody to Robert’s parents as she slid into multiple addictions.

The world had been kind to Smith, and she was brimming with trust. Russell had been primed for survival, trusting no one and empathizing with few. When Russell and Smith crossed paths, Russell wasn’t looking to help her; she needed a mark. But she framed her involvement in Smith’s life as an emergency intervention born of her concern. Did Smith have a way to get her hands on some money, fast? When Smith divulged her job loss, Russell encouraged her to apply for more jobs, stroking her ego like an old friend. Though Russell and Smith were roughly the same age, there was something maternal in her round face and soft, dark features. Russell had been groomed by her parents to understand how to win someone’s confidence, the gradual coaxing of attachment with the express purpose of betrayal. As the weeks grew into months, Russell turned herself into someone, maybe the only person, Smith could confide in.

Soon, with Russell’s encouragement, Smith got a new job, and they celebrated together. But it wasn’t enough money to save Smith, spiritually speaking. What started out as a $40 reading soon became $500, and then $1,500, to continue “the work.”

About three months into her relationship with Russell, Smith tentatively volunteered that her father had some money, and they came up with a plan to coax out some cash: Smith would tell her father that she was trying to improve her life, to get back on the right track. She would lie about needing help with tuition, therapy, and expensive sleep studies. Her family and friends had grown worried—Smith didn’t seem like herself—and her father agreed at first to help.

Smith had never lied to her father before, but Russell explained that if she didn’t do “the work,” then Smith’s father would get sick and die. And Smith loved her father, right? Smith nodded vigorously, the worst-case scenario never far from her mind. She felt lucky to have someone like Russell helping her.

Smith’s father started sending cash but was increasingly reluctant as Smith’s self-help bills mounted. Emboldened, Russell instructed Smith to tell her father that she needed $500,000 for a cutting-edge therapy that would erase her memories of an early-life trauma. Smith even sent her father a treatment plan she had assembled. Smith’s father demanded to speak with the therapist, so Russell had a relative play the part in a call that lasted more than an hour. Smith was also on the line, and when Russell didn’t think she sounded sufficiently distraught, Russell kicked her hard under the table to make her cry.

BY 2011, TWO years into their relationship, it was hard for Smith to keep up with the demands and expense of Russell’s spiritual program, despite the money she was taking from her father. Smith was now working on the soap opera One Life to Live. Crediting Russell with helping her land the gig, she handed over almost her entire paycheck. Smith had grown emotionally dependent on Russell; she had mostly stopped hanging out with her friends and kept her coworkers at arm’s length with a hollow smile. But Smith’s relationship with Russell was becoming increasingly fraught. At first, it had felt like Russell wanted to help her, that they were solving a problem together. But now, Russell was pushier and more explicit about all the terrible things that might happen to Smith and the people she loved if she didn’t unquestioningly cooperate.

As part of “the work,” Smith was told she had to clean Russell’s home and babysit her kids. Smith soon morphed into Russell’s personal assistant—booking vacations, arranging transportation, and running endless errands. She might be sent suddenly in the middle of the night to buy a TV or air conditioner, carrying the appliance on her back up the stairs to Russell’s apartment. Smith claimed Russell’s addiction to painkillers, muscle relaxers, and antianxiety meds inspired her to dispatch Smith to the city’s emergency rooms with a slew of made-up ailments—one time even telling her to pretend she’d been in a car accident—in order to get their hands on prescriptions.

Russell was surrounded by what seemed like a tight-knit extended family. In addition to her own parents and siblings, there was her common-law husband, Robert; Robert’s brothers, Tony John and Corry Blue; and the brothers’ parents, Archie and Candy. By Smith’s account, the dynamic was far from wholesome: There were fistfights, destroyed TVs, thrown furniture, and smashed bottles. Smith claims she saw Russell’s mother use a Taser on Russell’s sister. Over time, the violence was turned on Smith if she questioned or disobeyed instructions. Russell would insist that the “devil” was in Smith and that she had to be “cleansed” through beatings. One time, Smith says she was forced naked into a freezing-cold bathtub while Russell lit various objects and then shook and hit her as if it were an exorcism.

By this point, Russell had made two predictions that had (sort of) come true, and Smith was convinced of her psychic powers. Russell said that Smith’s father would have her incarcerated—a foretelling that was fulfilled when Smith went home and her father had her committed on a 72-hour psychiatric hold. When Smith was released from the hospital, she fled back to Russell, shaken by the prophecy.

In the midst of all of this, Smith found work in the wardrobe department of the TV series Madam Secretary. It was a dream job, but working full-time and often staying up until the middle of the night to meet Russell’s demands, Smith developed sleep-deprived vertigo. She was also drowning in debt. Smith says that Russell told her to rack up charges on her credit cards and even had Smith sign leases and rental agreements on the family’s behalf. She was told to buy a Bentley and pay for an apartment in Marina del Rey, California. The family took trips to Hawaii, Las Vegas, and Austin, attending Formula One races and a Stevie Wonder concert. Unable to keep up with payments, Smith saw her credit destroyed. But the family kept spending. Smith says Russell developed a taste for Louis Vuitton handbags and bought herself a $150,000 diamond ring. Her family posted their vacations on social media while Smith was back at home, paying for all of it.

All the anxiety of Smith’s early years in the city, when she was trying to gain a foothold in life professionally and personally, had been supplanted by the relatively straightforward but almost impossible aim of keeping one psychic satisfied. Smith was constantly doing cleanup on her relationship with Russell and her family. Russell’s mother and brother-in-law stole keys to Smith’s apartment, ensuring she had nowhere to hide. Smith says that, once, trying to track her down, they showed up and threatened Smith’s neighbor. It wasn’t just terrifying; it was embarrassing.

Smith soon realized it was futile to try to have any kind of life beyond Russell’s needs. She quit her job, despite feeling trapped between desperately wanting out of the relationship, shame at handing over so much control and stealing from her father, and terror at what might happen if she tried to leave.

BY 2013, SMITH’S father had forked over more than $1 million. His relationship with his daughter badly frayed, he was disappointed and done. But Russell told Smith “the work” still wasn’t finished. Smith had quit her job, so Russell came up with a new way for her to make money.

“Sex sells,” Russell told Smith, as if it were a demand of the universe and out of her hands. Russell instructed Smith to pack a suitcase and sent her to Washington, D.C., where she didn’t know anyone. She was instructed to start listing ads for sensual massage services—and the suggestion of more—on websites like Backpage.com. Soon, Smith was moving from hotel room to hotel room, seeing as many as 17 clients a day. Russell had become even more caustic and demanding, now frequently threatening violence. Smith claims that one night, Russell told her that if she didn’t come up with $10,000 quickly, Russell would infect her with HIV. Smith, estranged from her family and penniless, believed her. She hustled to make the payment.

Smith was in a perpetual state of fear. Her body was broken and didn’t even feel like hers anymore, and she was still chronically sleep deprived, with Russell and her family tag-teaming with nearly 24-hour demands. Soon, Russell told Smith that the money she was bringing in from “massage services” still wasn’t enough to keep the demons at bay. She would have to work harder, finagling jewelry and other expensive goods from her clients. She instructed Smith to tell them that she was in debt to people who wanted to hurt her. She should give her clients an opportunity to save her. Russell cracked open a window into her own grooming techniques, the manipulation tactics that had been passed down in her own family like a silver tea set.

After successfully conning a few men for extra cash, Smith met Daniel Zancan. He was married and had two kids and was the chief financial officer of his wife’s family business. Zancan, 34, with glasses and short brown hair, was, like Smith, relatively sheltered. He had graduated from a private high school, went to a good college, earned his accounting license, and made six figures. But despite his circumstances, he was looking for more—which led him to the racy ads on Backpage.com.

Zancan quickly became one of Smith’s regulars and, despite himself, fell in love. To him, Smith was wounded and delicate, someone who needed taking care of. To Russell, Zancan was another gullible mark, someone whose dissatisfaction could be easily exploited. She told Smith that her powers “saw money” around Zancan.

Smith was ordered to sell Zancan a tragic fictional narrative: that she had been abused by her father, who was now suing her. The court costs were bleeding her dry, and she had borrowed money from the wrong people—dangerous people, loan sharks. They wanted it back and sometimes held her against her will for days at a time, assaulting her. They threatened to do even worse.

Zancan jumped at the chance to be her knight in shining armor. But he had to be careful. He didn’t have a lot of money, and he couldn’t tip off his wife or in-laws. He started funneling small amounts to Smith—$2,000 here, $2,500 there. But in January 2017, Smith told him that she needed a lot more—$100,000. Russell had Smith tell Zancan that because she didn’t have the money, she could pay off the debt with a pair of expensive Rolex watches instead. Smith and Zancan made their way to a high-end jewelry store in northern Virginia, where Zancan filled out a credit application for a $10,000 line of credit—which wasn’t enough to buy even one of the watches.

Smith’s phone buzzed with texts from Russell’s family posing as the angry loan sharks, and Zancan was terrified about what the men might do to her. (Some of the calls and texts were coming from Florida, where Russell and her family were vacationing. Smith had booked their trip.) In a state of desperation, an idea was floated: What if he tapped into his employer’s ample resources? As the CFO, he had access to their bank accounts.

On January 11, 2017, Zancan embezzled $110,000 via a wire transfer he sent to Smith’s personal account. The next day, Smith converted the stolen funds into a cashier’s check, which she took to a check-cashing place in New York. Russell texted Smith to stay calm as she presented the large sum to the teller. “Don’t panic this is negativity it’s the devil trying to attack you and we will not except [sic] it rebuke it in the name of Jesus your powers are coming through,” dictated Russell. When the check was successfully cashed, Smith dutifully handed over every cent.

Privately, Smith was fighting her instincts. But she knew better than to cross Russell. On more than one occasion, Smith says she tried to walk out of Russell’s apartment, only to have Russell grab her by the hair and drag her back in, leaving bruises and threatening to kill her. Once, Russell issued a vague threat that her own young son would be harmed if Smith left. So Smith stuck with the plan, Russell telling her it would take just a little more money, that they were doing all of this to help Smith, and that things would get better.

THE RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN Smith and Russell, while dysfunctional and violent, was also strikingly affectionate. The now-yearslong spell was an incredibly potent mixture of fear and dependence. Smith didn’t just take Russell’s instructions; she clung to the tiniest morsels of care and actively sought Russell’s counsel. She spoke fondly of her to Zancan and other clients, telling them that the only bright spot in her life was her good friend, Gina. Isolated and unable to articulate how powerful Russell had become, she was intent on preserving a bond that seemed essential. The two were completely enmeshed, Smith doing Russell’s bidding for scraps of approval. It had to feel a bit like love when nothing else in Smith’s life did.

But Russell was firmly in control. Smith says that when it came to Zancan, Russell was clear: “Make sure he loves you enough that he would do anything for you.” Russell and her extended family continued spending lavishly, buying Louis Vuitton luggage, Tiffany and Cartier jewelry, and Patek Philippe and Audemars Piguet watches. Smith was forced to turn up the pressure on Zancan, telling him she needed $500,000 in cash.

One night, while Zancan was driving home from work, Smith called and said a loan shark named “Tony” (impersonated by Gina’s brother-in-law, Tony John) wanted to speak with him. Hammering home the threat, he said he knew where Zancan lived and worked. “Do I need to tell you where your kids go to school?” asked “Tony.” Zancan, panicking, agreed to steal the money and make the payment. Later, when he was en route to deliver the cash, one of Robert’s brothers took a picture of his license plate while he was in transit, which the family had Smith text to him. They wanted him to know that he was being watched.

Inspired by their new tactic, Russell and her family created additional characters to shake down Zancan. “Sammie” and “Santino” were even more sadistic; they gleefully told Zancan that they planned to beat Smith up—and worse. Zancan was breaking under the pressure. On February 5, 2017, Smith texted Russell in the middle of the night to tell her that Zancan was sobbing in their hotel room. “Tell him not to cry tell him that you love him very much,” Russell texted back. A few doors away, in their own room at the same hotel, Russell and Robert were taking videos of their young daughter posing with fat stacks of Zancan’s cash.

Later, Russell texted Smith to ask how Zancan was doing. Better, responded Smith. “We did good,” texted Smith. “Love you.” Russell texted back three crying-laughing emojis. “Love you,” she added. Russell then told Smith to delete her messages and get a burner phone. Shortly after, Tony John, impersonating a mobster in a call with Smith and Zancan, convinced Zancan to produce $1.6 million in gold bars.

Zancan was terrified but committed to a future with Smith. They would get through this mess and live happily ever after. On February 27, 2017, Smith texted Russell a picture. It was her left hand, her ring finger now heavy with a massive diamond engagement ring. Russell asked how many carats it was, and Smith guessed two, including the diamond-studded band. “Remember don’t fall in love and get too emotionally attached he only is doing this because you are emotionally supporting him,” texted Russell. Smith promised she was only “playing the part,” that she knew the difference between real and fake love.

Zancan had put aside $80,000 in gold bars that he hoped to use to start a new life with Smith. But soon after he put it in his car, Smith called to tell him a turf war had broken out between the gangsters. Santino had shot Tony. Santino wanted another $50,000 or Smith wouldn’t be allowed to leave. He threatened to rape her. Zancan liquidated the gold bars and handed $50,000 over to Smith at a Starbucks near Times Square. She gave it to Russell. Zancan and Smith drove to a hotel in Baltimore to spend the night, but not long after they checked in, the family started texting with more demands.

Zancan couldn’t take it anymore. He left Baltimore and started driving toward Texas. He was planning on collecting fake IDs there that he and Smith could use to escape for good. But when Zancan didn’t show up for work, his colleagues started digging around in his records and discovered the missing money. On April 6, 2017, Zancan was arrested. He had stolen more than $4 million, and he told the FBI everything. In a letter to the court, his parents suggested that Zancan’s vulnerability was being unusually trusting. “It is a good quality until it isn’t,” they wrote.

The FBI wanted to interview Russell and Smith, and Russell’s family hustled to come up with a cover story. They also decided that Russell, now 28, and Smith would get married, creating spousal privilege and ensuring that Smith couldn’t be compelled to testify against Russell. Smith was told to get burner phones to create “fake” conversations with Russell, crafting the impression that they were in love. They married at City Hall in New York.

But that wasn’t enough. According to Russell’s defense team, Robert’s mother, Candy, coerced Smith and her daughter-in-law to sign a notarized confession implicating themselves and absolving herself, her husband, and her sons of any illegal acts. Before Smith, now 32, went to her FBI interview in late April, the family threatened that she would spend the rest of her life in prison if she didn’t do exactly what she was told. Candy handed her two Valiums and told her it would help her “appear relaxed” during the interrogation. The Evans family (Robert’s brother) also made Smith sign a notarized confession and film a statement that absolved Russell and her family of any responsibility. But it wasn’t enough to assuage the family’s concerns that Smith might turn on them or that Zancan might successfully implicate them.

ON OCTOBER 19, 2017, a federal grand jury returned an indictment against Smith; she was arrested six days later. After eight years of terror, Smith felt a wave of relief as she was taken into custody. She was assigned to a maximum-security section of the D.C. Jail, where she bunked with a convicted murderer, and her stress-related chronic cough almost immediately ceased.

With so many details to disentangle, it would take another six months for a grand jury to return a 13-count indictment of fraud and extortion charges against Russell and her family. Russell and Robert split up, and the unified front fractured. Robert, his brothers, and his parents pleaded guilty to a litany of charges (Robert Evans and his brother Tony John Evans pleaded guilty to interference with interstate commerce by extortion; Corry Blue Evans pleaded guilty to bank fraud; Archie Kaslov pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit wire fraud; Candy Evans pleaded guilty to tampering with a witness by corrupt persuasion or misleading conduct) and accepted sentences that ranged from one to five years.”

Russell eventually agreed to plead guilty to one count of interference with interstate commerce by extortion. She convinced prosecutors to propose a limited prison sentence, in light of her dramatic upbringing and her promise to stay out of trouble. She received permission to live in Los Angeles, supposedly to help an ailing family member. But in 2024, Russell was arrested in connection to the young musician’s case. Prosecutors immediately recognized a pattern in the musician’s account: promising spiritual healing for steep fees, encouraging the theft of almost $200,000 from the musician’s wealthy father, and eventually driving her into sex work before her instincts had a chance to catch up. Russell’s L.A. arrest violated the conditions of her relatively lax sentencing deal, and it was revoked by the court. On July 18, 2024, she was sentenced to more than 10 years and five months in prison, which she is presently serving in Oklahoma. She was also ordered to pay $4,217,542.86 in restitution.

As Russell’s court battle played out, Smith was able to convince prosecutors that while she’d participated in extortion schemes, she’d also been a victim who had handed all her money and power to a woman who had threatened and exploited her. (The marriage between the pair was annulled in 2019.)

On September 9, 2024, Smith pleaded to one count of conspiracy to commit bank and wire fraud and was sentenced to time served and 36 months of supervised release. “Coercion is a complex thing,” noted Judge Tanya S. Chutkan, at Smith’s sentencing. “But what I have learned…is that under the right combination of stress, pressure, and psychological circumstances, seemingly normal people will do very abnormal things.”

Since her release from Russell’s grip, Smith has become an anti-trafficking advocate and now works for 3Strands, an organization dedicated to combating trafficking through education and reintegration programs. Last year, Smith provided testimony to a congressional task force in support of The Trafficking Survivors Relief Act, which was passed into law in January 2026 and allows victims of sex trafficking to have their arrest/conviction records vacated and expunged—Smith seems to have availed herself of this law as her criminal history is no longer publicly available. (The court records in her case were accessed and saved for this article before public access was removed.) Smith declined to comment for this article; instead, the above is based on the voluminous court records filed by both prosecutors and defendants in the Russell, Smith, and Zancan prosecutions.

In January 2026, Smith was pardoned by President Donald Trump.

It’s also worth noting that though Smith identifies as a victim of human trafficking, none of the people involved in her odyssey were charged or convicted of human or sex trafficking.

“There is no black and white survivor story,” she wrote in her testimony, alluding to the various definitions—both legal and informal—of the word. “There are all types of trafficking in this world.... I am determined to use my lived experience from these horrific years to bring meaningful change and protect others.”

*This story uses a pseudonym at the request of the victim’s lawyer.
