#4891. Tesla pushes Optimus deliveries to late 2027, says hands still a problem

Elon Musk now says Tesla will start delivering Optimus humanoid robots to outside customers around the end of 2027. On Tesla’s Q3 2026 earnings call, he said the hands, the robot’s durability and its AI all still need work before then.

Those are the same three problems every humanoid robot company is fighting. And despite Musk’s claim that nobody is close to Tesla, XPeng and Hyundai’s Boston Dynamics look at least as far along.

Musk said Tesla has started early production of Optimus on its high-volume line in Fremont, where Model S and Model X used to be built. Most of a line designed for a million robots a year is installed, but he said it will take at least a year, possibly longer, to reach that rate of about 20,000 units a week, because parts of the design are still changing.

He listed what has to be solved first: the AI, the electromechanical design, and reliability, including making sure the robot doesn’t wear out after a month of use. He expects those issues to be solved around the end of next year. That’s when Tesla expects to deliver Optimus to companies outside Tesla, starting with industrial jobs that are dangerous, repetitive or need to run around the clock.

When an analyst asked where the design was still changing, a Tesla Optimus engineer pointed to the hand as one of the hardest hardware areas, along with custom gears that still carry reliability concerns. Musk agreed the hand is the main issue, explaining that fingers need to be soft enough to handle delicate objects while surviving constant wear, and robots can’t heal like human skin can.

On the AI side, Musk said Tesla is still working through problems with the AI architecture. Tesla doesn’t have a fleet of robots collecting data the way its cars do for FSD, so it plans to build 10,000 to 20,000 robots and have them practice tasks in what it calls an Optimus Academy. Tesla also plans to put its AI5 chip in Optimus around April 2027.

Musk also promised an Optimus video within a month or two showing the robot doing tasks that aren’t pre-programmed. He argued that many humanoid demos look impressive but only run scripted routines that wouldn’t hold up in the real world.

None of this is new. Last month, we reported that Tesla had ramped Optimus to hundreds of units a week, but that the robots couldn’t generalize to new tasks. According to The Information, the hand and forearm had over 100 small parts assembled by hand, touch sensors had reliability issues, and the AI could take days to learn basic tasks.

Tesla’s own Q3 shareholder letter now calls the bots coming off the Fremont line “the first production-quality bots that we have manufactured.” So every Optimus before this quarter wasn’t production quality.

And the timeline keeps moving. In 2024, Musk said Tesla would build Optimus for internal use in 2025 and hopefully in high volume for other companies in 2026. In January 2025, he said Tesla would build about 10,000 robots that year, with “several thousand” doing useful work by year-end. He later admitted none were. Now external deliveries are a late-2027 target.

Musk said on the call that, to the best of his knowledge, “there is no one that is even close to Tesla” on a general-purpose humanoid robot. That’s hard to square with what competitors have shown.

XPeng turned on an automated IRON production line in Guangzhou in September, with more than 80% of core processes automated. IRON has 21 degrees of freedom in each hand and runs XPeng’s physical AI model on three in-house Turing chips. XPeng plans mass production by the end of 2026, deliveries in the first half of 2027 starting with stores and malls, and a European rollout in the second half of 2027. That’s a similar timeline to Tesla’s, if not slightly ahead.

XPeng is dealing with the same reality. It hasn’t shipped IRON to a paying customer, and its timelines have slipped like everyone else’s.

Boston Dynamics started producing its electric Atlas in January and says all of its 2026 Atlas deployments are already committed, including to Google DeepMind, whose AI models Boston Dynamics is integrating. In September, it opened a robot training center at Hyundai’s Metaplant in Georgia, where Atlas is learning to sequence car parts for the assembly line. Hyundai plans to deploy 25,000 robots across its plants over the next few years. Boston Dynamics also hired Milan Kovac, Tesla’s former head of Optimus, in January.

Boston Dynamics also seems to have taken a more pragmatic approach to hands, prioritizing sturdy grippers for industrial parts over human-like dexterity. That’s less impressive in a demo, but it’s a way around the problem Tesla says is holding it back.

My prediction is that Optimus will forever be delayed. It's like FSD in Tesla cars -- never quite good enough to really take off and always one or two releases away from fixing everything. At least a Tesla car with a broken FSD is still a good car. Optimus with a bad brain is an interesting-looking boat anchor.

Tesla is facing the exact same problems as everyone else: hands that survive real work, robots reliable enough to pay for themselves, and AI that can handle tasks it wasn’t trained for. Nobody has cracked generalization yet, Tesla included. The difference is that Tesla’s competitors aren’t telling investors they have no competition.

Based on what’s public, XPeng has a more automated production line and a similar delivery date, and Boston Dynamics is already deploying Atlas in a car factory with committed customers. Tesla may well have the most robots built, but building robots isn’t the hard part. Making them useful is.

Tesla has promised a video in a month or two. If it shows Optimus doing real, unscripted work, great. But we’ve heard about Optimus timelines before, and they’ve slipped every year. Why should late 2027 be different?

#4889. Scania speeds up switch to silent semi trucks with Chinese production

Record fuel prices driven by the dumb oil war in Iran are fueling a faster-than-expected switch to electric trucks in the world’s biggest freight markets – and Swedish heavy truck brand Scania is scrambling to meet demand with a new factory in China.

The Swedish truck maker is set to begin manufacturing battery-powered trucks at its new Rugao assembly plant in China as soon as it receives a license, according to Scania Chief Executive Officer Christian Levin.

In an interview given in Södertälje, Levin said he expects electric trucks to account for half of China’s market by the start of 2027. “We have had to speed up those plans,” Levin explained. “It’s always quite a complicated process in China to get licenses to do different things, but I have to say: it has moved much faster than we could have imagined.”

Chinese electric semi truck sales jumped almost 80% in the first half of 2026 compared to 2025, and are on pace to account for over 30% of all heavy trucks sold this year – and that pace is accelerating.

Scania built the Rugao plant last year, making it the Traton Group’s first wholly-owned factory in China. The facility will serve China and other Asian markets, and can build both conventional diesel and battery-powered trucks on the same assembly lines.

“It is happening quickly and that’s incredibly fascinating,” says Levin. “It means they have found a way to expand charging infrastructure and the power grid, which is the biggest challenge we have in many countries around the world, including Europe.”

#4883. The Men's Health 30-Day Workout Challenge

You can get moving to get in shape—but you have to commit.

SOMETIMES, THE MOST challenging part of working out is knowing what to do.

You might not have a definite goal in mind other than that you want to get moving, or that you want to look different by the time the summer season rolls around. That's okay. Not everyone is wired to constantly aspire to build muscle or run fast, following a detailed program designed to elicit peak performance and radical transformation. Just wanting to get active to live a healthier life is a worthy goal, especially if you're taking your first steps to make fitness part of your daily routine or recommitting to exercise after a break. But you have to be ready to commit to your new routine for it to be effective.

That's what the Men's Health 30-Day Workout Challenge is all about: doing something every day. Rather than limiting the focus to just one specific body part, muscle group, or type of exercise, as we have with our previous challenges, we're more interested in establishing healthy habits and introducing you to common exercise protocols that will be useful for the rest of your fitness life. Beginners can take the challenge and hold their own, while fitness pros can still push themselves to work to their full potential using these routines.

The plan is simple. You'll take on a new workout routine every day—but there will be some consistencies so you won't be constantly thrown into the deep end if you don't have a ton of experience. All of the workouts will be comprised out of a pool of just 11 exercises, which you can see demonstrated below by the program's architect, Men's Health fitness director Ebenezer Samuel, C.S.C.S.

Each week of the program will be focused on a different workout scheme, so you can get the swing of the structure and get comfortable within each protocol. The calendar will also be structured in a manner that allows you to flex all of your muscles, both figuratively and literally; Day 1 of each week will be focused on Mobility and Core, Day 2 is Upper Push/Pull, Day 3 is Lower body, Day 4 is a Mobility focus, Day 5 is Upper Push/Pull, Day 6 is an Upper/Lower/Core split, and Day 7 is all Core.

All you have to do is buy in. By Day 30 (or the bonus Day 31, if you're game), at the very least you'll have completed this challenge. If you put in max effort, you'll also be moving better, feeling fitter, and looking different than you did on Day 1.

For each interval workout, work for 40 seconds, then take 20 seconds off unless otherwise stated. Repeat for 2 rounds. The goal: Work for quality reps for each move.

• Minute 1: Spiderman Lunge to T-Spine• Minute 2: Hollow Rock• Minute 3: Plank Shoulder Tap• Minute 4: Mountain Climber

• Minute 1: Glute Bridge Reach• Minute 2: Bent-Over T• Minute 3: Pushup• Minute 4: Bent-Over T

• Minute 1: Squat To T-Spine• Minute 2: Paused Squat• Minute 3: Glute Bridge Right• Minute 4: Glute Bridge Left

• Minute 1: Squat to Reach• Minute 2: Glute Bridge Reach• Minute 3: Spiderman to T-Spine

• Minute 1: Spiderman to T-Spine• Minute 2: Bent-Over T• Minute 3: Close-Grip Pushup• Minute 4: Bent-Over T

• 1: Squat to T-Spine• 2: Glute bridge Reach• 3: Paused Squat• 4: Mountain Climber• 5: Bent-Over T• 6: Mountain Climber• 7: Pushup• 8: Mountain Climber• 9: Spiderman to T-Spine• 10: Mountain Climber

Work for 40:20 first time through, then 50:10

• Minute 1: Glute Bridge Reach• Minute 2: Hollow Rock• Minute 3: Shoulder Tap• Minute 4: Mountain Climber

You know the exercises you’re working with. Now things get fun. This week, we introduce you to AMRAPS, as many rounds as possible. You’ll work for 8 minutes in each workout this week, and your goal is to complete as many rounds of the circuit we lay out for you as possible. Don’t lose your focus on quality reps, but do aim to keep score.

• 5 Spiderman to T-Spine• 10 Glute Bridge per side• 15 Hollow Rocks• 20 Mountain Climbers

• 5 Glute Bridge Reach• 10 Bent-Over T’s • 20 pushups• 10 Bent-Over T’s• 30 Mountain Climbers

• 5 Squat to Reach• 25 Paused Squats• 25 Glute Bridges Left• 25 Glute Bridges Right

• 10 Spiderman to T-Spine• 10 Paused Squats• 10 Squat to T-Spine• 30 Mountain Climber

• 10 Spiderman to T-Spine• 10 Pushups• 20 Bent-Over T• 10 Close-Grip Pushups

• 5 Spiderman to T-Spine• 10 Paused Squats• 10 Bent-Over T• 10 Paused Squats• 10 Close-Grip Pushups

• 5 Spiderman to T-Spine• 10 Shoulder Tap• 20 Mountain Climber

This week you’ll learn the beauty of the EMOM, every minute on the minute. You’ll once again work for 8 minutes, completing the entire sequence of moves we give you every minute. Your goal: Finish all the work as quickly as possible (while still maintaining good form!) so you can rest until the start of the next minute.

• Minute 1: 6 Glute Bridge Reaches, 10 Hollow Rocks• Minute 2: 6 Glute Bridge Reaches, 15 Mountain Climbers• Minute 3: 6 Glute Bridge Reaches, 10 Plank Shoulder-Taps• Minute 4: 30 Mountain Climbers

• Minute 1: 5 Spiderman to T-Spine• Minute 2: 10 Bent-Over T, 10 Close-Grip Pushup• Minute 3: 10 Bent-Over T, 10 Pushup• Minute 4: 40 Mountain Climbers

• Minute 1: 5 Spiderman to T-Spine• Minute 2: 5 Squat to Reach, 10 Squats• Minute 3: 5 Paused Squats, 10 Glute Bridges per side• Minute 4: 10 Squats, 5 Glute Bridges per side

• Minute 1: 5 Spiderman to T-Spine• Minute 2: 10 Paused Squats• Minute 3: 20 Mountain Climber, 5 Hollow Rock

• Minute 1: 5 Spiderman to T-Spine• Minute 2: 25 Pushups• Minute 3: 20 Bent-Over T• Minute 4: 40 Mountain Climbers

• Minute 1: 5 Spiderman to T Spine• Minute 2: 10 Squats, 10 Bent-Over T• Minute 3: 10 Squats, 15 Pushups• Minute 3: 10 Squats, 20 Mountain Climbers

• Minute 1: 3 Spiderman to T-Spines per side, 6 Glute Bridge Reaches• Minute 2: 10 Hollow Rocks, 10 Plank Shoulder-taps• Minute 3: 10 Hollow Rocks, 20 Mountain Climbers• Minute 4: 25 Hollow Rocks

This last week, you’ll amp the intensity one final time, mastering the EMOM+1. You’ll once again train for 8 minutes each day, but each round, you’ll do a bit more work, by adding 1 rep to each of the exercises you must complete in every minute. That means the first minute of your workout may be easy, but the last minute will be ultra-challenging as you race against the clock to hit all your reps.

• Minute 1: 10 Plank Shoulder-Taps, 10 Hollow Rocks• Minute 2: 30 Mountain Climbers

• Minute 1: 5 Spiderman to T-Spine• Minute 2: 10 Close-Grip Pushups• Minute 3: 5 squat to reach

• Warmup Minute: 5 Squat to Reach• Minute 1: 10 Pushups, 10 Close-Grip Pushups• Minute 2: 10 15 Bent-Over T, 10 Mountain Climbers

• Warmup Minute: 5 Spiderman to T-Spine• Minute 1: 10 Mountain Climbers, 10 Pushups, 10 Squats• Minute 2: 20 Bent-Over Ts

Warmup Minute: 5 Spiderman to T-SpineMinute: 5 Plank Shoulder Taps, 10 Mountain Climbers, 5 Hollow Rocks

You’ve learned and utilized four different styles of quick-workout training, now let’s sneak in three more workouts that mix-and-match these principles.

#4880. Volkswagen is launching its most affordable EV yet in 2027, starting at around €20,000

Volkswagen’s upcoming electric car will be smaller and lower-priced than the ID. Polo, starting at around €20,000 ($22,500).

The new Electric Urban Car Family is the Volkswagen Group’s answer to Chinese automakers like BYD: a new lineup of compact, entry-level electric cars.

The lineup currently includes the Volkswagen ID. Polo, ID. Cross, plus the Cupra Raval and Skoda Epiq, all based on the same MEB+ platform.

After launching the lower-priced base versions of the ID. Polo and ID. Cross, starting at €24,995 and €27,995, respectively, Volkswagen is preparing to introduce an even smaller, more affordable EV in 2027.

Volkswagen revealed the ID. EVERY1 concept car last March, a preview of its upcoming entry-level EV that will arrive in 2027 starting at around €20,000.

The ID. EVERY1, which is expected to go on sale as the ID. Up! next year, is “the last piece of the puzzle,” VW brand CEO Thomas Schäfer said, as it aims to offer the widest selection in the volume segment.

With a length of 3,880 mm, the entry-level EV is positioned between the former Up! (3,600 mm) and ID. Polo (4,053 mm). Although that is tiny, VW said it will offer space for four passengers and a luggage compartment volume of 305 liters.

Volkswagen has yet to reveal details, but the €20,000 EV is expected to use the same 37 kWh LFP battery as the base ID. Polo and ID. Cross to keep costs down.

The ID. Polo with the 37 kWh battery has a WLTP range of up to 334 km (207 miles), so the smaller model will likely offer around the same or slightly more range.

Volkswagen said it will offer at least 250 km (155 miles) of range. It will also use a new 70 kW (94 hp) electric motor, enabling a top speed of 130 km/h (80 mph).

The production version of the ID. EVERY1 will be one of nine new models VW plans to launch by 2027.

Volkswagen delivered on its promise to launch the ID. Polo with the 37 kWh battery for under €25,000. Will it do the same with the new entry-level model at around €20,000? We will find out shortly.

It will be produced in Portugal, this has been confirmed ages ago.

According to Spanish auto magazine Autofácil, Volkswagen could manufacture the €20,000 EV in Spain, although Volkswagen has yet to confirm a production site.

The Group currently produces the ID. Polo and Cupra Raval at its Martorell plant, while the ID. Cross and Skoda Epiq are manufactured at the Navarra plant, both in Spain.

Volkswagen’s new Electric Urban Car Family is off to a promising start, securing nearly 150,000 orders after series production began in June.

While those in the US will miss out on the new entry-level EV, Volkswagen is launching the ID. Tiguan in 2027 as a replacement for the ID.4.

#4879. The 7 Best LED Face Masks for Men in 2026, According to Experts

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

For battling blemishes and signs of aging, there are few better at-home tools.

AS SOMEONE RAISED on slasher horror movies, I was always going to gravitate towards LED face masks. But while their creepy Jason Voorhees-at-a-rave look is what initially grabbed my attention, the skincare benefits are what sold me on the products. LED face masks combine the firming power of anti-aging products, the depuffing of eye cream, the energizing boost of moisturizers, and the breakout-fighting strength of acne washes—making them one of the most versatile grooming tools out there.

LED masks use specific wavelengths of light to penetrate the skin and trigger cellular changes, according to dermatologist Dr. Hannah Kopelman, MD. This can include stimulating collagen production to reduce fine lines and support firmer skin, as well as treating acne-causing bacteria and calming inflammation to promote a clearer complexion. Some devices offer all of these benefits, while others are laser-focused (get it?) on just one or two. The key is to know what each is capable of and what service you’re looking for.

Dermatologist Dr. Brian Toy, MD, warns that the market is flooded with LED face masks that vary greatly in quality and effectiveness, so it’s best to start your search as informed as possible. To temper the confusion, I went ahead and used myself, along with fellow Men’s Health writers and editors, as guinea pigs. This way, you’ll know what works and what is merely an overpriced Halloween mask.

We gave Shark Beauty CryoGlow a 2025 Men’s Health Grooming Award barely a month after it was released; that’s how great this LED mask is. It offers four separate treatment options that cover anything you could possibly want out of an LED face mask. The Better Aging setting uses red and infrared light to reduce wrinkles and firm skin, while Skin Clearing mode combines blue, red, and infrared light to fight blemishes and even tone.

The Skin Sustain maintains glow with a quick mix of all three LED wavelengths, and Under-Eye Revive uses cryotherapy-inspired cooling to depuff and tighten the under-eye area. You can also use this under-eye cooling ability combined with the other treatments, which roll out in three increasing levels of chill. Each is between four and eight minutes, meaning you don’t need to dedicate much time to combat whatever issue you’re after. Under-Eye Revive, you can do up to 15 minutes if you’d like, but you only need five to be effective.

Dr. Peterson Pierre, MD, FAAD, likes that this device uses red, blue, and infrared lights so that you can get a full smorgasbord of benefits, like combating acne, fighting signs of aging, reducing inflammation, and helping regulate oil production. He also digs the cooling feature and three levels of intensity. I’ve been using my CryoGlow for months, and have seen a noticeable change in the smoothness and clearness of my skin, as well as reduced redness, using The Better Aging and Skin Clearing settings. But where I saw the most immediate results was with eye puffiness.

If I’m ever running on limited sleep or recovering from a night out, I pop the mask on, and after a few minutes of Under-Eye Revive mode, I look like I’ve actually slept. The light from this device doesn’t feel glaring when you’re wearing it, so I was able to successfully walk around and multitask during my treatments.

Plus, as someone who is generally sensitive to light, it also feels a lot less intense than other options on this list, and never inspired headaches of any kind. Not to mention, it’s easy to adjust and fits my face perfectly. I only have a few nitpicks. Given the expansive options and customizability of this mask, there is a handheld controller attached to it to help you navigate. While this makes firing up the device super easy and you don’t need to rely on an app, the controller can be a bit awkward to deal with while you’re in treatment.

You can’t put it in your pocket without accidentally changing the setting, so you have to hold it, which limits the multitasking you’re able to do. Also, the mask is bulkier than its main competition for best overall, the Dr. Dennis Gross Face Mask. But when you consider that the CryoGlow is also the cheapest full-face option on this list, it’s a fair trade-off.

Read More: Shark CryoGlow LED Face Mask Review

Dr. Kopelman has been recommending this LED mask to patients for years. She likes that it is FDA-cleared and offers both red and blue light; however, what she likes most about it is that it consistently delivers results. In terms of effectiveness, it’s equal to the CryoGlow. The only reason it just missed out on the top spot is that it’s over $100 more expensive and offers fewer additional treatments, like under-eye cooling. Beyond that, I find it just as successful at battling blemishes and signs of aging as the Shark Beauty.

Plus, the treatments are shorter, and you only need to wear this for three minutes a day to see results. Unlike many other options, like the CurrentBody or FAQ 202, which are made of more flexible material you can mold to your face, this design is rigid. While that may seem like a drawback, I loved it. Of all the LED masks on this list, I found Dr. Dennis Gross to be the sturdiest, and it fit my face perfectly. It’s slim, without feeling flimsy, and doesn’t weigh down my face like other similarly sturdy masks that tend to be a bit heavier, such as the Theraface Mask.

That being said, I possess an incredibly average build and face shape, so if you fall outside of those parameters, the singular and unadaptable design of this mask might not be as perfect a fit. Unlike the CryoGlow, it’s wireless when you’re using it and can be conveniently charged with any USB-C charger. This helps when traveling, though the solid design poses some challenges if you’re tight on storage space.

Similar to the Dr. Dennis Gross mask, this device is crafted with a hard, contoured shell; however, it’s far less slim. But it trades off this added bulkiness with its vibrating ability, which soothes facial tension and boosts blood flow around the eyes, brows, and scalp. It offers red, blue, and infrared light therapy to target acne, improve skin tone, and increase collagen production.

You can choose between three- or nine-minute treatment modes, though we found the longer sessions to be more effective. Sure, this mask can feel a bit heavy or bulky on the face, but the results are legit. In fact, some effects can be seen immediately, and they only increase from there. “After the very first time I used it, my skin felt softer, and my pores looked smaller,” says Senior Gear and Commerce Editor Ryan Brower.

“Over time, my skin tone looks more even, and my skin appears to be firmer, smoother, and less puffy.” He adds that the massaging, vibrating feature is relaxing, although it can feel ticklish or even chill-inducing at times. Since it sits close to your ears, it can also get a bit loud, especially when multitasking. Still, it’s really easy to switch between settings, turn on and off, and choose the massage style you want.

If you’re solely looking to combat puffiness, dark circles, and wrinkles, Lumin is the way to go. Sure, it looks straight out of an abandoned Lone Ranger In Space reboot, but there is no device better at rejuvenating the skin around the eyes than this mask. One tester saw noticeable improvements after days of use with this device. “I naturally have darker circles, but after consistent daily use for about a week, I saw a noticeable difference in the brightness and overall alertness of my eye area,” she says. The mask stays in place well, and the soft silicone padding makes it comfortable throughout each session.

Its adjustable design also ensures it fits all face shapes and sizes with ease. The same tester also saw a brighter tone and smoother skin after a couple of weeks of daily use. “While I don’t personally have under-eye wrinkles, I can see how this would be especially helpful for someone who does or for anyone who spends a lot of time in the sun,” she says. Not to mention, the Luminator is quick and easy to use—just three minutes a day with an auto timer.

Our testers found that this FAQ mask makes a strong impression right out of the box with its ultra-thin, flexible design, which feels more like a high-end sheet mask than a tech device. You’ll need to download the app to get the most out of this tool, however. There’s a single button on the mask, but without the app, we found that it was nearly impossible to remember its function or how to power it off.

Once the app is set up and the mask is synced, navigating the features becomes straightforward—just select your desired treatment and that’s it. Despite being covered in tiny LED lights, the mask feels surprisingly lightweight and comfortable. During the 15-minute session, testers reported no heat or noticeable sensation on the skin and even forgot it was on while doing other tasks, such as reading. The mask stays comfortably in place, even when looking down at a book or phone.

We also appreciated the included cleaning spray. For anyone with sensitive or breakout-prone skin, keeping the mask clean is essential, and the spray makes that simple. After each use, we cleaned and dried the mask before placing it in its pouch, which securely holds the device and makes storage hassle-free. One minor concern was the split at the bridge of the nose—designed for flexibility—which left one tester wondering if that area was receiving full treatment. Still, this didn’t deter them from continuing to use it.

Women’s Health fitness contributor Nicolette Accardi says that the Qure Pro LED Mask has taken her nightly skincare regimen to the next level. After a month of use, she saw a dramatic difference in her skin’s appearance. She used to struggle with oily skin and frequent breakouts, but since regularly using the pink LED light setting, she says it has significantly reduced her sebum production. “I'm also approaching 30 (yikes), so I've been using the red LED light setting as well to help combat fine lines and reverse skin aging,” Accardi says.

Each session runs for three minutes and automatically shuts off when it’s done, so you never have to worry about timing it yourself. It’s perfect for anyone who wants results without the hassle. It’s one of the easiest, most low-maintenance skincare tools out there at a relatively low cost. That’s not to say $380 is cheap, but when it comes to legit, effective LED masks, you won’t find many other options under $400. It’s really just this and the CryoGlow.

If the more rigid masks, like CryoGlow, Qure, and Dr. Dennis Gross, are too bulky for you, but the FAQ is too small for your face, Currentbody will be your best option. This mask offers the most flexibility, with a silicone design that easily molds to the contours of any face, ensuring full coverage. This is as long as you tighten the straps. I’ve been lazy a few times with that, and it will start slipping off your face mid-treatment. In addition to the flexible fit, this mask feels super gentle on the face.

One of our testers used it only days after getting eye surgery with no issue. Didn’t bother her eyes one bit. That being said, it takes up to six hours for a full charge, which can be a bit annoying. This is the longest charge time on this list by a few hours, to be clear. I’m the type of person who pushes off charging a device until I absolutely have to, so this long charge time usually results in me skipping a day of treatment. But if you’re a better planner (to be fair, it’s a low bar compared to me), it’ll be less of an issue.

Depending on what skin issues or concerns you’re looking to address with your LED face mask, you’ll want to focus on which treatments it offers. This is driven by the color of light the device uses, which dictates its benefits. Some on this list offer multiple services, while others zero in on one. These are the common options:

While some are comfortable and allow for multitasking, there is no getting around the fact that you’re wearing a large light on your face. As a long-time migraine sufferer, having a light this close to my eyes for too long can be a trigger. But even if you’re perfectly fine with prolonged light exposure, you’ll want to know what the time commitment is before buying LED face masks, as they’re most effective when used regularly. Some are as long as 25 minutes, while others can be as short as three minutes. Keep in mind that not all are meant for everyday use; some (especially the ones with longer treatment lengths) may only need to be used a few times a week for max efficiency.

When shopping for an LED face mask, choosing a device that’s FDA-cleared is essential, says Dr. Kopelman. This ensures the product meets fundamental safety standards for consumer use. To be clear, however, FDA-cleared is not the same as FDA-approved—the latter involves extensive clinical trials and rigorous testing. Currently, no LED face masks on the market have achieved FDA approval.

For now, stick with FDA-cleared options, which means the device is proven to be as safe and effective as another legally marketed product. You might also see terms like FDA-registered or FDA-listed, but these simply indicate that the manufacturer has notified the FDA of the product's existence—there’s no review or evaluation involved. Because of that uncertainty, you won’t see any of those on this list.

There are a lot of LED face masks out there, and like any trendy tool, not all are created equal. So, before putting any to the test, I consulted with a panel of dermatologists on which devices were legit and which they recommend. They also advised me on what to look for in a quality LED face mask and the brands to focus on. Based on this intel, I, along with other Men’s Health writers and editors, put several masks to the test, evaluating each device’s effectiveness, ease of use, and how comfortable it was to wear.

As many LED face masks do not offer immediate results, we used each one for at least one month to ensure enough time was given to gain any possible benefits. Following this extensive research and testing, I landed on these seven LED face masks as the best for men in 2026.

The dermatologists I spoke to for this story were clear on this: you should be cleaning your device after every use. If you don’t, bacteria, oil, and product residue can build up on the surface and transfer back onto your skin, causing irritation or breakouts, which may ironically be what you were hoping to minimize by using an LED mask in the first place.

Dr. Kopelman says that LED masks should always be used on freshly cleansed, dry skin to ensure the light penetrates as effectively as possible. After the session, apply your serums and moisturizers—doing it beforehand can block the light and reduce its benefits. A hydrating serum like hyaluronic acid or a peptide-rich cream works especially well to complement the collagen boost from the treatment, Dr. Kopelman says.

According to Dr. Toy, be sure to skip any products that might react to light. For example, because retinol and vitamin C serums are photosensitizing, they’re an absolute no-go before any LED treatment. Dr. Chacon adds that reflective products like heavy oils or sunscreens should also be avoided during use as they can scatter the light and disrupt the device’s effectiveness.

#4877. 10 Best Sweatpants for Women, Tested By Fashion Experts

Our favorite pair on this list is from Vuori.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

After testing more than 50 sweatpants over the past two years, I can confidently say today’s best sweatpants for women are no longer reserved for bed rotting on lazy Sundays. I’ve worn top-rated styles with a white t-shirts, styled them with my go-to wool coat for running errands, and paired them with an oversized hoodie while WFH. The difference between frumpy and fashionable comes down to fabric, fit, and style: today’s standouts are made with soft, stretchy, and moisture-wicking materials that are a cinch to move in and hold their shape well. And thanks to activewear all-stars like lululemon and Alo Yoga, modern sweats feel polished enough to wear beyond the couch—without sacrificing comfort.

To find the best sweats, the WH fashion team did the legwork (get it?) for you, trying tons of popular pairs on a variety of body types. We landed on oversized, fuzzy styles made for couch hangs to sweat-wicking joggers that can handle anything your day throws at you. Keep reading to find out what to consider when shopping—and which pairs deserve a spot in your cozy drawer.

If you’re looking for a simple pair of sweats that you can wear with anything, this is our top pick. I have these in both the jogger and wide-leg versions, and both are in my regular rotation all fall and winter. Plus, they have such a flattering drape that doesn’t emphasize my hips or belly. “It has that classic old school sweatpant texture that’s soft and thick,” says Saladino.

I love the extra-soft cotton material that feels so cozy to slip into on chilly mornings and lazy evenings. They’re made from a mid-weight terry cotton that feels as comfortable as your college hoodie, but has enough heft to them that they don’t cling or ride up. They have a thick, fuzzy interior and a smooth exterior, so they feel lived-in from the moment you put them on.

“I really like that these sweats hit just above the ankle,” says Saladino. You can wear them with socks and sneakers or pair them with mini Uggs for a laid-back but put-together look. They also have a classic elastic waistband with no tie for simplicity—sometimes you don’t need a ton of bells and whistles to look put together! Plus, we love the roomy pocket on these.

There are tons of color options to choose from, too. If you want something that goes with anything, you can opt for the washed grey or black shades. But, they also come in options like hot pink or bright red, which Saladino says add a fun pop of color to an otherwise basic sneakers-and-sweatshirt look.

Our favorite part about these pants is that they come in three different fits: Regular, petite, and tall. And, to top it all off, we agree that the wide size range is helpful, too. We like to size up in these for a cozy, roomier fit. Because they’re nice and structured, they don’t look like they swallow you up when you go for a bigger size.

These sweatpants are lightweight enough to wear in the summer, but cozy and thick enough to be your go-to in the winter thanks to the super soft cotton and elastane blend. I find them to fit similarly to the Gap pants above, but they’re just slightly thicker, and they have a drawstring on the outside of the waistband, which I like. Also similar to the Gap pair, they’re super soft and cozy. At the same time, they’re breathable, so you can totes wear them to a workout class and be dry by the time you walk out the door.

The size options that these sweatpants come in also blew us away, ranging from XS all the way up to 3XL. Rest assured, you can find a size that fits you like a glove. We found the fit to be loose enough for comfort, but snug around the waist and at the ankles for a more tailored fit. Style contributor Lily Wohlner usually wears hers with sneakers, but says slides or boots in the winter work great, too.

Like the Gap sweats, these pants have side pockets, but we found them sturdier and deeper. They can hold our phones without an ounce of fear that they’ll fall out.

Surprisingly, we prefer these sweatpants in a snugger fit. When too oversized, they can add extra bulk to the legs. For a more flattering look, we recommend sizing down.

Even though Skims is known for shapewear, the brand also makes some great relaxed fits. And these sweats in particular have become a personal favorite. I love how loose and flowy they are in the legs—ICYDK, this relaxed fit is back in style—but they have a stretchy elastic waistband that keeps them snug around the waist.

“I run super hot, so I appreciate sweats that are on the thinner side like this pair,” Wohlner says. “I can even sleep in these without getting too overheated.” They almost feel like you’re wearing a long pair of boxers with their lightweight material.

These definitely run large, so I recommend sizing down one size—or even two sizes if you want them to feel a bit more snug. Wohlner usually wears a large in sweatpants, but went with a small in these. They’re still roomy but not so baggy that she wouldn’t wear them out for a walk or a quick grocery run.

There are a few straight leg options on this list, but I love Alo’s Straight Leg Sweatpants as they are suuuper soft and lightweight for lounging or heading out for the day. They come in a ton of color options, too. They look great with most casual fits, but our style team loves wearing them with Alo’s color-coordinating jackets and hoodies for a chic, monochrome vibe.

They are made with a French terry cloth, and Juric says this makes for a great fleece lining that is super breathable. They have an oversized look, but if you want them to fit more snugly you can size down or even twice. I’m into the oversized look and love that these sweats don’t fit too tight on the lower belly, since other popular sweatpants I’ve tested can emphasize that area too much. Wohlner also prefers them a bit bigger, as she can always roll down the waistband for a more snug fit around the hips.

“The only downside to these sweats is the length; the pants go well past my ankle, making them hard to wear outside,” says Juric. Nevertheless, Juric notes that they are great to lounge in at home. “Plus, I think sizing down would’ve solved the length problem,” she says.

Saladino describes these sweats as dreamy on the inside and cool on the outside. “These are the types of sweats you can wear outside of your house and look pulled together,” she says. She touts the retro stripe and the vintage-y broken-in look for giving them a more street style vibe. They come in tons of different colors to choose from, too. Although they’re a bit pricier, she says that Aviator Nation’s striking style and premium materials are worth the extra spend.

These sweats are more fitted around the waist, and get fuller as they go down the leg for a roomier, more comfortable fit. The interior is buttery soft and fuzzy for extra comfort. They do run small, so beware of that while shopping. Saladino went up to a large and says they’re the perfect fit. They also have a slight drop-crotch so you never have to worry about them riding up or being too tight around that area (IYKYK).

We’ve worn these in public and they look great with everyday fits like a wool coat, a chunky knit sweater, and paired with socks and sneakers.

Like Adanola, Aritzia has a great mix of loungewear, activewear, and streetwear. And these sweatpants won us over the second we tried them on. We love that they’re incredibly comfortable and very chic. The flared cut is super on-trend, and it doesn’t look overly tufted like most fleece sweatpants and jackets we’ve seen, making them pretty dressy, Wohlner says. I wear mine out and about all the time.

“The fabric is pillowy-soft and the fit is just the right amount of roomy,” says Juric. “Thanks to the fleece fabric, wearing these pants literally feels as if you took the coziness and warmth from your bed on the go.” Hint: if you want something that feels like a warm hug, these are your winners.

I personally like that these sweats have a skinny drawcord waistband, as I find it looks a bit more flattering if you want to wear them low-rise. They do fit on the looser side, so size down if you don’t want them to look too baggy.

Winter is on its way, which means we’ve been on the hunt for a pair of sweats to throw over our shorts or leggings to and from the gym, and we’ve officially found our favorite pair. We love layering the Andie Oversized Fleece Sweatpants over shorts when we run to and from the gym as the temp drops. They’re warm enough to protect from the cold, but lightweight enough to keep us from overheating and feeling sticky. And, of course, we throw them on during cozy days lounging at home.

We love these for layering as the fabric is unlined and relatively thin, so they don’t add much bulkiness to the clothes we have on underneath. Thanks to the blend of modal and spandex, they’re super breathable and stretchy, so they almost feel like nothing when you have them on. Plus, if you get a little sweaty, the fabric is moisture-wicking (big ups!).

However, if you’re looking for an ultra-warm pair of sweatpants to keep you cozy during long treks outdoors, you might be better off with another pair on this list (like the Aritzia Cozy Fleece Mega Flutter Sweatpant).

When I first felt these sweats in our fashion closet, I knew they were going to be the winner for the softest option on this list. And when I tried them on for the very first time, my suspicions were confirmed. In comparison to all the others, these feel like butter, but they’re pretty thin and lightweight, so they don’t feel too heavy. I usually find joggers to be less cozy than wide-leg sweatpants, but these fleece joggers feel like absolute heaven—I’ve even fallen asleep in these a few times.

And after Saladino tested them for a few weeks, she had similar things to say. “These are hands-down the softest sweatpants I have ever worn,” she says, adding that they feel like a giant hug. “They’re perfect for super-cold days where you want to snuggle on the couch.” We agree that these are more suitable for lounging than for errands or the gym, as they err on the casual side.

Saladino likes wearing these a bit bigger so they feel even more cozy, and the medium was perfect for that. They run a bit large, so opting for your normal size will give you that slightly oversized fit that we recommend. Even though they’re baggier, they don’t slide down at the waist. If you prefer your sweatpants to feel snug, opt for a size down.

Softness is a must when it comes to sweatpants, and stylist Jackie Schiavone says the right material is key.

We tested an array of styles and silhouettes for this guide, but Appelt says the most important thing to keep in mind while shopping for sweatpants is your body type:

Sweatpants are meant to be oversized, so you don’t have to worry as much about fit, as, say, jeans. But it’s important to make sure the pair you choose is still flattering. Look for a body-skimming fit that doesn’t cling too tightly to your thighs while sitting comfortably at your waist or hips. Also, pay attention to length. You don’t want your pant leg to drag on the ground while you walk, so consider options that come in petite, regular, and tall lengths, depending on your height.

I'm a style writer who's been testing activewear for years. I’ve covered everything from the best workout leggings to the best hoodies to the most comfortable slippers. For this story, I combed through my extensive testing, researched the best women’s sweatpants, and called in a bunch of sweats to try. I also consulted with two style experts on what to consider when shopping for sweatpants. Style contributor Lily Wohlner and stylists Kristen Saladino, Rose Lauture, and Alexandra Juric also weighed in on their favorite options.

For the last year and a half, we tested more than 50 sweatpants across seasons, from brisk winter mornings to sunny summer eves. What matters most? Adaptability. These picks strike the perfect balance between comfort, movement, and style. Expect breathable cotton blends, moisture-wicking trims, and chic silhouettes from top brands like Vuori, Alo, and Skims.

#4874. A Reader’s Guide to the Many Sexy Roles of Alexander Skarsgård

Hollywood initially tried to make the 50-year-old star into a traditional hunk. He got weirder—and hotter—instead.

FAR TOO OFTEN, today’s Hollywood hunks deny their beauty to play a cavalcade of schmucks, freaks, and losers with funny accents, hiding in prosthetics because they think this will transform them into “serious” actors in the public eye. But this strategy doesn’t always pay off. Leo spent two hours and 42 minutes running around in a plaid bathrobe and messy man bun only to lose the Best Actor Oscar to Michael B. Jordan, who played a smokeshow vampire with a spit kink (and his identically sexy twin).

It’s best not to underestimate someone with undeniable sex appeal and unquenchable blood lust, as Alexander Skarsgård knows all too well from his years playing Eric Northman on True Blood. The role not only made Stockholm’s native son a household name in America, but an instantly recognizable sex symbol. Not that he needed much help from Hollywood. Skarsgård is 6'4" of muscle with anime bone structure. He’s 50, but doesn’t age in human years. He makes us mere mortal men all look, and feel, lesser than. The scion of Swedish acting royalty comes from a place where everyone kind of looks like that, yet he’s been named Sweden’s Sexiest Man Alive five times.

“After my first job, I was on a stupid ‘sexy hunky hot list’ and then people didn’t take me seriously,” Skarsgård told the The Sunday Times in 2022. “If you want characters with depth but have been labelled ‘a dude who takes his shirt off’, you’re not going to get those offers.” At the time, he was promoting The Northman, for which he’d packed on 25 additional pounds of muscle to play a Viking warrior prince, and spent most of his screen time shirtless, delivering the exact sort of performance that theoretically typecast him in the first place.

From scanning his filmography, it’s clear that at a certain point, Skarsgård decided to lean into his lot in life as an unapologetic sex symbol. Over the past two decades, he’s slowly gravitated toward roles that don’t attempt to soften or normalize his hunkiness, portraying a diverse range of characters who all just happen to be ridiculously hot in films and television shows that play with his beauty, what it means, and how it messes with the rest of us.

In his latest, Wicker, Skarsgård plays a literal object of desire, the purest distillation of his on-screen persona as a sweet and (still, somehow) sexy magical dildo who loves doing chores and adores his fishmonger wife (Olivia Colman), causing hysteria in a village full of dumbasses who have no idea how to treat or fuck a woman. In other words, he’s Alexander Skarsgård.

The Male Model: Zoolander & Zoolander 2 (2001 & 2016)

Ben Stiller’s comedy classic is built around the premise that Jerry Stiller’s son and Owen Wilson and Benedict Cumberbatch are male models. A fun piece of trivia is Skarsgård was inserted as one of Derek’s United Nations of conventionally attractive roommates. Baby faced Meekus is hilariously bad at bitchy teenage girl humor and loves orange mocha frappuccinos. He gets in a gasoline fight in the first installment that results in a fiery death, but returns for the sequel in a brief cameo, perfectly cast as the original man.

Skarsgård became a star when this show was a very good gothic soap opera people held in the same regard as many of the HBO classics that were on at the time, but it has faded from memory due to completely spinning off its axis in later seasons. But his role as Eric Northman, a sexy, menacing Viking prince who carries himself with regal arrogance when he first washes up in Louisiana, remains an indelible performance. He’s a kind of Magneto/Lestat figure, who believes in vampire superiority and humans primarily as food, then slowly reforms.

This remake of the 1971 Sam Peckinpah classic is a bad, hamfisted W. Bush era culture war movie (released three years late), in which James Marsden, as a pretentious, Harvard-educated lib Hollywood screenwriter, is pitted against Skarsgård, who plays a God-, guns-, country music and football-loving redneck. But the use of Skarsgård is symbolically correct: As a rugged man’s man who works with his hands, hulks over Marsden’s effete snob, and represents all Marsden’s shortcomings and insecurities.

The Charismatic Cult Leader: The East (2013) & The Stand (2020)

Two roles that trade on Skarsgård’s magnetism, casting him as cult leaders. One is Benji, an eco-terrorist ringleader in The East, which was overshadowed by Kelly Reichardt’s superior eco-terrorist anti-thriller Night Moves from the same year, but is also very good. Skarsgård begins the film as a hirsute, politically radical Jim Morrison. The role generally strips a lot of his raw tools away but he proves he still has the juice, running his operations with the certitude of a self-righteous zealot, taking full advantage of his implicit understanding that everyone will do what he says because they all want to fuck him.

That same energy is twisted evil in the less-than-stellar and largely forgotten Paramount+-produced adaptation of Stephen King’s The Stand from 2020. Skarsgård is having a blast here, clearly tapped in and comfortable with the cheap, fatty, made for TV vibes. He plays Randall Flagg, an infamous demonic anti-Christ figure in King lore, who also swaggers around making dark, grand pronouncements because he knows everyone is dreaming about him…and wants to fuck him.

The Mythological Figure: The Legend of Tarzan (2016) & The Northman (2022)

These are the two loin cloth roles that make best use of Skarsgård as physical clay. The first was a bid for a franchise at a more conventional phase of Skarsgard’s career. It’s a horribly problematic text about a Lawrence of Arabia raised by gorillas in the Congo, released at what was probably the latest moment in modern history anyone could’ve possibly thought this IP could still work in any context. And yet, Christoph Waltz is the bad guy, Margot Robbie is Jane, Samuel L. Jackson turns in a peak performance. It doesn’t really matter, because the movie doesn’t work. The one very funny, deeply horny beat, however, is Tarzan and Jane’s meet cute, when Robbie happens upon a still uncivilized, dirt and grime covered Skarsgård in the jungle, who emerges from the brush, towers over her, then sniffs her from head to toe, which is a shameless, incredibly erotic romantasy/soft porn scenario.

The Northman on the other hand, rules, and might just be the best movie in director Robert Eggers’s burgeoning and impressive filmography. I still wonder to this day how it wasn’t a bigger deal (likely the mid 2022 Covid-era release date, but still). Skarsgård leaves it all on screen in this folklore epic, near naked in the snow, in the mud, in the waves, shredded and extremely believable as a raider scaling ramparts with a battle axe, lurching through villages as they’re pillaged and burned.

The Alpha Scumbag: Big Little Lies (2017-2019)

“Biggest scumbag Alexander Skarsgård has ever played” is quite a distinction, but it has to be Perry Wright, a manipulative, abusive, domineering, womanizing monster who entwines magnetic, toxic sex with serial spousal abuse in David E. Kelly’s Shakespearean, rich, white wine-momsploitation thriller. He plays one of the few believable on-screen partners Nicole Kidman has ever had, arm candy who wears the fuck out of tailored suits. He’s a striking contrast to the show’s other husbands, all older boring, brunette, beta boys. He’s a perfect-from-a-distance husband and father, the on-paper exemplar of a certain anachronistic masculinity, and also the epitome of damaged male evil. Which is why Perry’s Orient Express style group murder is the climax of the first season of the show.

The Tech Demigod (The Odin of Codin): Succession (2018-2023)

A highly unlikely proposition. Harry Melling (who most probably still know best from his role as Dudley Dursley in the Harry Potter films) is Colin, a nebbishy mama’s boy with an aptitude for devotion in a barbershop quartet. Colin’s meetcute is delivering a back alley blowjob with little preamble to Skarsgård’s Ray, the hung final boss of leather daddies in the sweetest BDSM rom-com since Secretary. As Ray, Skarsgård communicates almost entirely via squinting, grunting, monosyllabic responses, and direct commands, yet is a completely alluring masculine ideal. His hobbies are waxing his motorcycle, watching shit on his phone while he eats, wrestling in assless unitards as foreplay, and reading Knausgaard. You can smell the sandalwood, cedar and tobacco wafting off the screen.

In which Skarsgård finally, inevitably plays a robot. This is a darkly comedic, but also occasionally saccharine, Apple TV+ series about a Wall-E war machine. His character, known only as Murderbot, has found a way to disable the guardrails that would otherwise force him to obey protocols programmed by the nefarious Weyland-Yutani style corporation who created him, and uses this freedom to consume our garbage TV shows. Murderbot expresses a professed disinterest in humanity, and hates eye contact; It’s a weird, flat, funny performance that ultimately lands halfway between Pedro Pascal in The Mandalorian and Peter Weller in Robocop. Skarsgård is a completely believable robot in a show that also serves as a metaphor for autism.

#4873. Race Day Roundtable: Speed Stories From Runners Who Raced in On’s Cloudboom Strike 2

Three athletes competing at three different distances share their experiences—and satisfying finishes.

Running “fast” is objectively subjective. What’s fast for you could be slow for another runner and impossible for someone else. Fast can even mean something different for individual runners depending on factors like where they are in a training cycle, if they’re coming back from an injury, or the distance they’re running.

Some runners equate fast with a specific pace-per-mile. Brooklyn-based fashion designer Florence Canonoy, for example, said it’s about seeing her paces drop on her tracking app month after month. “I just run to feel good, and then I look at my watch and it’s like 8:15 [per mile], and I’m like, ‘oh, I’m getting fast,’” she told Runner’s World.

For others, like Mollie Kaplan from Florida, running fast has nothing to do with the time on her watch. “When I’m feeling confident and happy, I feel like that’s when I produce my fastest times—when I’m not putting as much pressure on myself,” she said.

And for Long Islander Chris Chung, fast is a feeling: “When I’m doing interval workouts, that’s what fast feels like to me,” he said. “It’s feeling the wind in your face, in your hair, and just feeling like you’re floating.”

Regardless of how you define it, most runners would agree that their footwear plays a role in just how fast they feel on a particular day, especially race day. Below, Canonoy, Kaplan, and Chung share what they each learned pursuing personal goals in different races—all while wearing the On Cloudboom Strike 2.

A content creator from Fort Lauderdale, Florida, who played lacrosse in college and has completed four marathons.

Distance raced in the Cloudboom Strike 2: marathon in Chicago

An industrial designer and content creator from Jericho, New York, who’s been running for 10 years and did his first marathon in 2025.

Distance raced in the Cloudboom Strike 2: half marathon in Vancouver, British Columbia

A fashion designer from Brooklyn, New York, who ran casually in high school and college and began taking running seriously this year.

Distance raced in the Cloudboom Strike 2: 5K in New York City

Race goal: Push herself while returning from a hip flexor injury

This interview has been lightly edited for clarity and concision.

Co-created with athletes for marathons and half marathons, featuring our CloudTec Sphere™ cushioning system for a fast ride and Helion™ HF hyper foam for energy return.

Mollie: My first marathon in New York City in 2024 was my fastest. I’ve been wanting to PR since then. But going into Chicago, we had a yellow warning [weather alert] with less than ideal conditions. So I was a little frustrated because after training all summer in the heat, I was really excited to finally do a cooler marathon and was definitely prepared to PR. But I took the pressure off myself the last two weeks before the race. My goal was not to look at my watch. I just wanted to go based on feeling and not to freak myself out.

Chris: This was my first half marathon back from an injury, a stress fracture in my femur. I hadn’t run 13.1 miles in a year, so I was like, ‘I’m just going to let it come to me and see how I feel. Let me just keep it below 1:50.’

Florence: I was taking my last couple races easy, but this was the one where I actually felt really good. So I was like, ‘Okay, let me push for it.’ It was one of my first races where I really took it seriously.

Mollie: I felt pretty strong from the start and I knew that it was going to be a good day for me. I can usually tell from the first mile. And the Cloudboom Strike 2, they kind of give you speed without trying. So they propel you forward a little bit, which is really great.

Chris: I started at the front and got caught up in the wave of people going out quickly. Within the first quarter mile, I was running PR pace at 6:20s and thinking, ‘I’m definitely not holding this because I haven’t trained like this at all.’ So I pulled myself back. I knew there were some hills on the course, so I just kept it effort-based. The Cloudboom Strike 2 maintained its responsiveness even when slowing down a little bit. I really liked how the rocker didn’t feel too aggressive, so it didn’t feel like I had to stay up on my toes the entire race. But at the same time, the roll-off felt really smooth and helped me maintain my cadence fairly well. The upper was comfortable and didn’t feel overly tight. It had some leeway in it and it felt light and breathable.

Florence: At the beginning, I felt really good, so I started running really fast and the Cloudboom Strike 2 had really good return. I felt like I was bouncing the entire time and it was easy on my hips, so that was great. It was also pretty breathable, which helped because that day it was really, really hot out.

Mollie: I saw my mom, my sister, and my boyfriend four times throughout the course, and every time I saw them, I had a boost of energy right after. Mile 20 was a turning point for me because I was like, ‘I’m still feeling so good I could speed up at this point,’ which I’ve never felt before in a marathon. And then when I finally looked at my watch at mile 24, I knew I had two miles to go and was super close to PR. That’s when I started picking it up, and it was just such a great feeling.

Chris: There’s a section of the race where you run along the seawall in Vancouver; you’re literally running alongside the ocean. Since I train solo, sometimes I love no crowds and the quietness of everything. I turned off my headphones for a little bit and listened to my own footsteps, my own breathing, and just took in the view. And you have that wind coming off the ocean a little bit, and you just feel like you’re kind of cruising.

Florence: In the middle and at the end, obviously the people cheering really helped. But I also felt like my stride was really good, where I was just bouncing and flowing, and I didn’t feel any wobbliness or stiffness. I have shoes that are a little bit too stiff, and I feel something in my body or my hip, but Cloudboom Strike 2 was really good towards the end.

Mollie: [In the last third of the race], they felt really good and comfortable and my body was feeling good, which was a really good sign at that point in the race, but the shoes still felt super springy. And when I started to push the pace a little bit, it just felt like a natural stride.

Chris: Other racing shoes can be really firm and aggressive. With this shoe, I feel like that little extra cushion really felt good for where my fitness was. It’s a little deceiving because it can feel like your foot’s sinking in, but at the same time you’re getting that responsiveness back from it.

Florence: I think it did help in terms of the cushion. There was a big hill in Harlem, so that was a little bit difficult, but the shoe helped propel me forward.

Mollie: I PR’d by three minutes, which is super close when you really think about all the little things that could go differently. I’ve cried crossing the finish line of every single race I’ve run, especially those last 100 meters. I get so emotional thinking about what I just accomplished before even the PR. Just completing a marathon is something so incredible and something that I’m so proud of every time I do it. I think about all the time and work that I put in, the months leading up to it. It’s just a very overwhelming feeling as you’re crossing the finish line.

But when I saw my time, I kind of stopped a little bit because I was so excited and so happy. I’ll definitely be wearing Cloudboom Strike 2s again, and I would definitely recommend them to anyone who’s in the market for a new pair of shoes to race in.

Chris: I know I have the speed in me; I just didn’t know if I had that fitness in me. So it was a good feeling to finish in 1:37. I was happy that I was able to push my body a little more than I had in the past year.

Florence: I went into the race not looking at my watch. And when you start to hear the cowbells, that’s when I started feeling really good and I was like, ‘You know what? I’m almost done. I see the finish line right there, so might as well sprint it.’ So that’s what I did. It felt amazing. Everybody was cheering.

Mollie: Something I’m working on is having confidence in myself from the first mile rather than waiting till mile 13. I tend to second guess myself, especially on the start line. I can tell myself, ‘It's okay if you go a little slower, if you don’t hit your goal.’ And anyone else who’s training for a marathon or looking to achieve the same goal, I would say just have confidence in yourself. Enjoy the journey. Celebrate the little wins, especially in your training cycle.

Chris: To get back to that speed, I know I have to put in more speed workouts. And it’s about playing the long game, too. You can’t force it.

Florence: This race taught me the importance of relying on feeling and not paying too much attention to my watch. When I look at my watch a lot, I tend to run a bit slower. But when I just focus on myself, whatever’s playing in my earphones, and just feeling good and just doing it, I run faster. We have our goals, but rely on how you feel. I think the number one thing is just enjoy it.

A highpoint of On’s Cloudboom Strike 2 is the technology. CloudTec Sphere™ helps keeps your legs fresher for longer by absorbing more of the impact, so you can retain your speed deep into a marathon.

#4872. The Man Behind Fashion’s Most Dazzling Spectacles Turns His Attention to the Art of Light

For as long as he can remember, Alexandre de Betak has been entranced by light. As a 10-year-old, he rewired his Paris bedroom so that visitors had to be buzzed in, greeted by shifting colored lights. He went on to found Bureau Betak, a set design agency that transformed the runway with its megawatt spectacles for clients like Dior, Gucci, Jacquemus, and Fendi. De Betak estimates that he produced “thousands” of fashion shows—including Saint Laurent’s spring-summer 2020 ready-to-wear extravaganza, for which he bathed the Eiffel Tower in golden light, and installations for Rodarte featuring fluorescent and neon tubes.

A new truss light sculpture by Alexandre de Betak, seen here in a 17th-century Swedish castle

Now, de Betak, who sold his company in 2021, is turning the spotlight on his own creative practice. On November 5, he opened his first solo exhibition of artworks at Salon 94 in New York. The electronically programmed Truss Light Sculptures are inspired by the scaffolding and fixtures of his early runway shows and in some cases literally made from them. “That equipment is old-fashioned now, but I wanted to honor it,” de Betak says. “And I liked the irony that I spent so much energy over the years trying to hide it.”

On view at Salon 94’s Upper East Side town house through December 19, the exhibit presents two series. In the gallery’s contemporary space, the first is composed of freestanding and wall-mounted aluminum structures fitted with LED bulbs. The upstairs Stone Room, a historic space with Caen stone plaster walls and arched windows, is the backdrop for a second series of versions in bronze. To make them, de Betak had a French foundry recast each part down to the smallest screw by hand, a process that sometimes required more than 20 molds.

A pair of wall-mounted sculptures in aluminum

The light sculptures, which vary from sconce-like creations to hulking constructions out of a sci-fi movie, have a sly sense of humor and a human quality. This is especially true when they come to life, thanks to a remote-control-operated system that activates light sequences that glow, sparkle, thrum, or react to ambient noise, “whether a whisper,” de Betak says, “or extremely loud music.” For these effects, he drew on his stage work, where he was renowned for cueing, or choreographing, light and sound. “I’m interested in the ephemeral nature of what this equipment was made to show—whether a fashion show or a ballet,” he says. “At a moment when everything is virtual, I think it’s more important than ever to create things that produce a live emotion.”

Salon 94’s founder Jeanne Greenberg Rohatyn observes that de Betak’s sculptures are equally powerful switched on or off. Unlit they remind her of David Smith artworks or Russian constructivism. Lit, and with synced sound, they evoke the theatricality of stage performers. “Alex has spent his career building structures that disappear into someone else’s spectacle,” she says. “Here, the structure is the whole point.”

#4871. An Easy 3 Miles with On’s Cloudsurfer 3

After years of stubborn loyalty to another brand, could one city jog make a longtime runner reconsider his shoes?

After just a mile in On's Cloudsurfer 3, it dawned on me—I’ve been far too hard-headed when it comes to my choice of running shoes.

For years, I held steadfastly to a particular brand and style, year after year, run after run. When one pair wore out, leaving my shins aching and feet tender, I’d quickly order a replacement online without even a thought of pivoting. Different colors and patterns kept it interesting, but that was the extent of my athletic audacity.

Truthfully, it wasn’t about brand loyalty. I wouldn’t dare try another shoe by the same company. It was more a case of preferring what I had grown used to in the past decade over the potential thrill of experimentation.

When I was asked to take On’s Cloudsurfer 3 for a jaunt, I was skeptical. Not that the shoes couldn’t or wouldn’t be great—it’s On, after all, a company renowned for exceptional technology and an ultralightweight feel to their sneaks—but that they’d be able to win over someone like me.

Still, I was game. The assignment called for my honest opinion during a three-mile run, and I was ready to break out of my rut (or at least try to). So I laced up and headed out on a beautiful early-fall Sunday afternoon in New York City. Here’s how it went.

I was intrigued even before I took my first step. Putting on Cloudsurfer 3, it immediately felt lighter than my go-to shoes. That surprised me, considering the minimal weight of my faves is what originally attracted me to them. The knit-mesh on the outside of the Cloudsurfer 3 was light and airy, and the inside was plush in all the right places (including the generous ankle collar) without being overbearing.

Yet, I knew the bigger test was to come. As a long-time sand volleyball player, I’ve developed a harder-than-necessary plant of my foot when I run, so I tend to need soft cushioning from a shoe.

Heading outside, I took a breath and set off down the sidewalk. The first strides were cautious, as I focused on the new sensation. The initial feedback was encouraging. It all felt effortless and soft, which I later would learn was due to On’s proprietary Surreal™ Superfoam with CloudTec®. I knew of On’s “run on clouds” tagline, but now I was feeling it in action, and I liked the smooth, soft ride I was experiencing.

I was a half-mile in when I hit my first red light—an unavoidable hazard of city running—giving me a moment to stop and reflect. “That was easier than usual,” I thought. I appreciated the secure feel of my ankle without it being too constricting, and my foot didn’t shift at all in the propulsive phase of my gait. The toe box was nice and comfy.

Pleasantly surprised so far, I changed my route on the fly and headed into Central Park. I wanted to test out the Cloudsurfer 3 on the oval around the Great Lawn . . . and enjoy an uninterrupted 0.55-mile loop.

I was breathing a little heavier at this point, but I noticed something about the shoe: It gave me the sensation of running downhill, even on a flat surface. I also felt what I’d call a “rebound” effect as each foot touched down and lifted off. This energy return made me feel faster than usual, with a burst of extra power on my “swing” phase and increased confidence in my mechanics. Could the Cloudsurfer 3’s mere 10.8 ounces per shoe be the difference maker?

I don’t know if it was the refreshing chill in the air, the clearer path than I’m used to in the city, or an extra “oomph” that the shoes’ softness provided, but I did a doubletake when seeing my 10:02 split time at the end of the second mile—well ahead of my typically slow 11-minute pace.

After two treks around the Great Lawn, I was back on the paved trail that leads out of the park. The sweat was beading despite a comfortable temperature in the high 60s, but I was enjoying the workout.

By the last mile, my legs were feeling good thanks to the easy two miles prior. I was in “go” mode and barely noticed my shoes. I decided to switch up my routine and finish with a series of sprints on the city blocks—fast bursts between intersections, with short rests at red lights.

Everything was still flowing smoothly: an effortless “lift” on each step, a seamless heel-to-toe transition, and no reverberations from the hard sidewalk and street underfoot. The last third of the run seemed to fly by, and I was more than happy with yet another sub-11-minute mile. I also realized that a fresh scrape on my ankle from a volleyball match earlier in the week, which I had been worried about aggravating during the run, was completely pain free; there was no chafing whatsoever.

When I took this assignment, I knew I’d likely be impressed with On’s Cloudsurfer 3. This is no ordinary sneaker, after all, but one designed with Swiss precision and an array of features celebrated by regular Joes and top-tier marathoners alike.

What I wasn’t quite ready for was the thought that maybe, just maybe, it was time to move on from my old standbys. I do know one thing as I reflect on the experience: My daily runs will be in On’s Cloudsurfer 3 because its soft, smooth ride made this run feel effortless.

#4870. Kia believes it has a way to beat China’s cheap EVs in Canada

Kia is betting its new lineup of affordable EVs, like the EV3, can beat the incoming wave of Chinese models in Canada, but affordability is only one part of the equation.

After launching the EV3 in Canada in August, Kia said it was the lowest-priced electric vehicle on the market, starting at CAD $39,744.

It may not hold the title for long, though. Canada struck a deal with China earlier this year, allowing up to 49,000 electric vehicles to enter the Canadian market at a 6.1% tariff rate.

According to Kia Canada’s COO, Elias El-Achhab, the company sees the deal’s timing as an opportunity.

“I thought it was just a bonus,” El-Achhab said during Automotive News Canada’s Retail Forum this week.

Kia is “trying to be the first affordable EV brand in the country,” he said, but that doesn’t necessarily mean just offering the lowest-priced vehicle. The Korean automaker is focusing on offering EVs at an affordable price that still come with the tech and features buyers want.

The EV3 (check out our review) joins Kia’s other mass-market electric vehicles, including the EV4 and EV5, that are now on sale in Canada.

When asked whether Kia could face more competition from China because of its positioning as a low-cost brand, El-Achhab said: “I actually think the opposite.”

“Because we are more affordable … and I will reiterate, it’s more of a value equation that we offer,” he explained during the Forum.

While Kia still offers vehicles across all powertrains, El-Achhab said that around 90% of those who buy an EV tend to stick with it.

At Kia’s national dealer meeting last week, he said the company’s vision had plenty of support, adding that orders for the EV3 and EV5 are already backed up.

The EV5, Kia’s midsize electric SUV, starts at CAD $43,495, and the EV4 starts at CAD $38,995 in Canada.

Although Kia delayed the EV4 for the US “indefinitely” and has no plans to bring the EV5 to the States, the EV3 is now on sale. Starting at $29,890, the 2027 EV3 is among the most affordable electric vehicles currently available in the US.

The 2027 Kia EV3 is available in four trims with front-wheel-drive and all-wheel-drive (AWD) powertrain options in the US and Canada.

Buyers can choose from two battery pack options. The lowest-priced EV3 Light FWD model uses a 58.3 kWh battery and delivers up to 221 miles of range. The Wind, Land, GT-Line, and GT use a larger 81.4 kWh battery that delivers up to 321 miles of range on a single charge.

Inside, the interior features Kia’s new ccNC (connected car Navigation Cockpit) with standard wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto.

The setup includes nearly 30″ of screen space combined, including dual 12.3″ driver display and infotainment screens, and an added 5″ climate control display.

They will be fine until various Chery sub brands, geely, byd show up with extreme values. Ev3 seems to be doing ok in Europe as maybe there is some brand loyalty. I haven't heard good things about Kia dealers in Canada. If geely can bring the ex2 in for under 30k cad. I'm not sure ev3 can hold it's own. Kia might have to reduce prices then like they have done and then sure. They just need to bring value.

All EV3 variants come with a built-in NACS port so that drivers can charge at Tesla Superchargers without a separate adapter.

The 58.3 kWh battery can charge from 10% to 80% in 29 minutes using a 350 kW DC fast charger, while the 81.4 kWh battery takes around 31 minutes.

All EV3 models come with standard i-Pedal 3.0 one-pedal driving, vehicle-to-load (V2L), and Smart Cruise Control (SCC).
