#4856. ‘I Got Rhabdomyolysis From a Kettlebell Workout Even Though I’m an Experienced Exerciser’

There’s a difference between pushing yourself and overdoing it.

I could tell something was off one morning during the summer of 2020 when I went to the bathroom and saw what appeared to be grainy bourbon swirling around in my toilet bowl. (Sorry if I’ve forever ruined your fave whiskey for ya!) Startling, oh yes. Thinking back, I had been nursing achy hamstrings following a kettlebell workout a few days prior. And since my pee certainly hinted that something wasn’t working right internally, I suspected the two were connected.

Until that workout, I hadn’t picked up a kettlebell in months. It had been my primary form of exercise for six years—I even got certified to teach it—but I was starting to burn out, so I swapped in a less intense Pilates practice. Now I was ready to ease back into the swing of things (key word: ease).

I began with a 30-pounder and did one-minute intervals of swings, squats, and presses, eventually moving up to 45 pounds. I’d worked with that weight before—but again, it had been awhile. I left the gym hobbling (oh, my hammies!) but otherwise fine.

The soreness lingered but wasn’t bad enough for me to cancel Saturday Pilates. A stretch might be good, I told myself. But I woke up the next day to my unfortunate bathroom sitch.

I was vaguely aware of the condition known as rhabdomyolysis, in which injured muscle tissue breaks down and releases its contents into the bloodstream, potentially damaging the kidneys. But I figured there was no way my 25-minute kettlebell sesh could have been intense enough to cause that level of harm. Yet I found myself Googling “that thing when you work out too hard” (who can remember the word rhabdomyolysis?). One of the first symptoms I came across: dark, brownish-colored urine.

After some initial testing at urgent care, I was referred to the ER, where doctors measured my creatine kinase (CK)—an enzyme found in your muscles that, when elevated, may indicate damage. I learned just how injured I was: A healthy adult’s CK level falls between 22 and 198 U/L (units per liter); mine was a whopping 90,000 U/L.

When I was told I would have to be admitted for at least a day, it was a strange pill to swallow. I wasn’t suffering from any other symptoms, like dehydration, nausea, or faintness. Yet I spent the night in the hospital spooning an IV bag to flush my kidneys fast enough to avoid damage. (Renal failure can be one of the more serious side effects of rhabdo.)

I was told to take six weeks off from exercising. When I did venture to my first hardcore class (boxing), I sneaked a peek at my pee for days afterward, just to make sure everything seemed A-OK. Fast-forward a year later, and I’m healthy as ever.

I get it: You feel a sense of pride when you fight through the so-sore feels. But you’ll come back stronger if you take a day off when…

Sweat on Sunday and still achy by Wed? Cue to cool it.

If you’ve played tennis forever but feel zapped during a longer or hotter practice, it might be your bod asking for a break.

Let’s say you have been training for a race and can’t run as fast as you did last week, but your regimen is the same. Build more recovery time into your plan.

FYI, exercise-induced rhabdo isn’t terribly common—about 12,000 cases are diagnosed annually in the U.S., according to a study in BMJ Open Sport & Exercise Medicine. But Todd Cutler, MD, an internist at NewYork-Presbyterian/Weill Cornell Medical Center, says nurses in his ER noticed an uptick in rhabdo cases that coincided with the recent rise in popularity of high-intensity cycling classes.

It’s not typically an exercise newbie who gets injured, either; it’s often a healthy, relatively fit person who pushes themselves to extremes the first time they try a new workout (or when they return after an absence). It makes sense, given my experience. “If you weren’t fit in the first place, you wouldn’t have been able to do the exercise,” says Dr. Cutler. In other words, my underlying health allowed me to reach the point of overexertion.

There’s a fine line between pushing yourself (which nets you gains) and going overboard (which leads to injury). The tipping point is different for everyone, which is why it’s key to be in tune with your body. (Hamstrings feel as if they’re under a blowtorch? Put down the weight!) If you’re trying something new or going back to working out after a hiatus, ease into it, advises Lauren Borowski, MD, a sports medicine specialist at NYU Langone Center for Women’s Sports Health.

My new mantra: Match workouts to current ability (no matter your past experience). And…rest days are clutch. Take them. The kettlebell will still be there tomorrow.

#4849. BMW is already discounting the new iX5 with a $1,000 loyalty bonus

The iX5 is set to go on sale in early 2027, but BMW is already offering a loyalty discount to sweeten the deal for those looking to stay with the brand.

Following the new iX3 and i3, the iX5 will go on sale in early 2027 with BMW’s Neue Klasse-inspired design, technology, and sixth-generation (Gen6) eDrive system.

The iX5 is the first fully electric BMW X5. For its fifth generation, the BMW X5 will be available in gas, plug-in hybrid (PHEV), and battery electric (EV) powertrains in the US. Overseas markets will also see diesel and hydrogen fuel-cell versions.

While the gas-powered 2027 X5 40 xDrive is now available, the electric iX5 still says it’s “coming in 2027” on BMW’s website.

BMW is already sweetening the deal with a $1,000 loyalty discount for returning buyers or lessees, according to a memo CarsDirect reviewed that was sent to dealers.

Although a $1,000 credit may not seem like much, it’s twice what BMW is offering for the 2027 iX3. The discount doesn’t require a trade-in and can be stacked with other offers.

BMW’s loyalty discount provides a cash rebate off the MSRP when you buy or lease a new BMW through BMW Financial Services and have owned or leased another BMW within the last 12 months.

The iX5 doesn’t have any other current discounts or lease offers, but keep an eye out closer to launch.

Earlier this week, BMW showcased the i5’s fast-charging capabilities for the first time during a media event in Southern California with IONNA and Alpitronic. During the event, the iX5 60 xDrive hit a peak of 464 kW, which BMW said enables it to add up to 170 miles of range in 10 minutes.

The iX5 60 xDrive uses a massive 144 kWh battery, which BMW estimates will offer up to 435 miles of range.

Powered by a dual-motor all-wheel-drive powertrain, the electric SUV delivers a combined 578 hp (425 kW) and 593 lb-ft of torque, and can go from 0 to 60 mph in 4.4 seconds. It can also tow up to 6,000 lbs.

Inside, the iX5 adopts BMW’s Neue Klasse setup, with a wide 17.9″ central touchscreen and BMW Panoramic Vision that spans the base of the windshield. Buyers can also add the optional 14.6″ passenger screen.

Measuring 197.2″ in length, 78.7″ in width, and 68.9″ in height, the iX5 is about the size of the Porsche Cayenne Electric.

You have to wonder why Tesla’s name keeps coming up in this discussion, too. This BMW has a net battery capacity of 144 kWh and achieves an energy density Tesla hasn’t even come close to matching. Tesla wanted to get there, but the 4680 battery has been a technical disaster. Even the Cybertruck has a significantly smaller battery. On top of that, the BMW is highly efficient, thanks to its electrically excited synchronous motor (EESM), which doesn’t use rare earths. We’re talking about cutting-edge technology here, in a completely different league from Tesla.

BMW will officially launch the 2027 iX5 50 xDrive in the US in the first quarter of 2027, starting at $79,800.

The iX5 is the first all-electric BMW model produced in the US. Production is set to begin at its Plant Spartanburg in South Carolina by the end of the year.

Don’t want to wait for the bigger iX5? You can check out BMW’s smaller iX3 and see what’s available near you below.

#4847. A Former College Athlete’s Battle With Depression

He spent years trying to power through his depression, cycling through several traditional oral antidepressants, before finding a medication that worked for him.

JEREMIAH FELT GLUED to his couch, too sad and unmotivated to move. He was supposed to be getting ready for his wedding—a day when he expected to feel more confident than ever. Instead, his groomsmen had to come to his apartment and help him get there. A former college athlete, Jeremiah was still a big guy, and it took all of them to lift him from the couch and carry him out the door.

It’s not what you think. Jeremiah had absolutely no doubts about marrying the love of his life. He was in the throes of a depressive episode, one of many he had experienced dating back several years. For Jeremiah, becoming a husband meant becoming a provider and protector. But on the day he was supposed to step into that role, he was the one who needed help—and he felt ashamed.

The wedding-day episode was just one part of a much longer struggle. Jeremiah’s symptoms first appeared in college and worsened after graduation. When he entered the workforce, his symptoms worsened and he became exhausted and increasingly apathetic—to the point of neglecting his hygiene. Eventually, he became too depressed to get out of bed in the morning and lost his first job.

In 2012, Jeremiah was officially diagnosed with major depressive disorder (MDD), a mental health condition that can have a significant impact on daily life and make it difficult to find motivation or energy for self-care. Over the next nine years, persistent symptoms made it difficult for him to maintain employment, and he eventually went on disability.

DEPRESSION IN MEN often hides in plain sight. In 2021, 6.2 percent of U.S. adult men and 10.3 percent of U.S. adult women experienced a major depressive episode, according to the National Institute of Mental Health.

Those numbers tell us how common depression is, but not what it looks like. Men and women can experience many of the same symptoms, including sadness, hopelessness, fatigue, changes in sleep, and loss of interest in favorite activities. However, depression often shows up differently in men. Feeling sad or emotional isn’t always the main symptom. For many men, symptoms can show up as headaches, digestive problems, tiredness, irritability, or long-term pain. Feeling isolated or seeking distractions to avoid dealing with feelings or relationships can also be signs.

According to Craig Chepke, MD, DFAPA, a psychiatrist and medical director based in Huntersville, North Carolina, men may have a hard time talking about their feelings and asking for help, making diagnosis and treatment difficult. “Depression in men is often missed or misread, including by men and others close to them, because it doesn’t always look like what people expect depression to look like,” he explains. “Instead of sadness, it may show up as irritability, anger, withdrawal, or self-medication. Sometimes it takes an ultimatum from someone who cares about them just to get them into the office. Depression is a medical condition, not a character flaw, but I hear men with depression say variations of the same thing over and over: ‘If I was just stronger, I’d be able to handle this on my own.’”

Jeremiah agrees. “You feel like less of a man, like you should be able to just power through somehow, or snap out of it,” he says. “But you can’t. You don’t. Depression affects your confidence in every aspect of your life. It becomes a dehumanizing experience.”

BEYOND HIS OWN self-doubt, Jeremiah had a hard time finding healthcare providers who would take his symptoms seriously. He dealt with therapists who minimized his struggles. One provider even attributed his symptoms to restless legs syndrome.

At times, Jeremiah felt that some doctors viewed depression as a “woman’s disease,” subtly calling his masculinity into question. Being a Black man added another layer as he navigated a healthcare system that didn’t always understand his experience.

He experienced more difficulty when he opened up to loved ones. “Being a man is lonely in general. There are very few men you can talk to beneath the surface level about things even though you call each other friends. I shared my struggle with MDD with my two closest friends, and it kind of freaked them out,” he says. “We didn’t talk much after that for about a year.” He received a similar reaction from cousins and extended family members, who weren’t sure what to say or whether to treat him differently. Things improved once they saw that his personality hadn’t fundamentally changed.

Jeremiah’s marriage, however, became a turning point. His wife, a clinical therapist, was uniquely positioned to recognize his condition. Starting around 2016, she began noticing subtle changes, how he would pick up and lose interest in activities and hobbies, and how Jeremiah would withdraw into himself around the house. It was then that she encouraged him to seek professional help. But asking for help was only the beginning. Finding a treatment that adequately addressed his symptoms would take years.

IN 2021, JEREMIAH was diagnosed with treatment-resistant depression (TRD), which affects about 30 percent of people with MDD. TRD is generally defined as MDD that has not resolved after trying at least two traditional oral antidepressants. “By the time someone checks off medication after medication on an intake form, they’ve usually lost something more valuable than time,” Dr. Chepke says of people living with TRD. “They’ve lost hope that anything can get better.”

Jeremiah knew his feelings were real. “TRD is a bully and it will hit you in the face from the moment you wake up,” he says. “Your best days are not behind you. You’re just going through something that a lot of men go through and just aren't able to admit it. You’re working to hold onto the life you want to live, not just your health, but your lifestyle, who you want to be, and the type of man you want to become or already are.”

For a while, Jeremiah kept trying new medications and started losing hope when they didn’t work. But with help from his wife and doctor, he found a different path.

LOOKING BACK, WHAT mattered most to Jeremiah was his wife’s consistent support through the process. In the early years of treatment, she helped him remember appointments and his medication schedules that kept him moving forward when motivation was scarce. Jeremiah’s doctor recommended he try SPRAVATO® (esketamine), an FDA-approved nasal spray for adults with TRD, used alone or with an oral antidepressant.

It is not known if SPRAVATO® is safe and effective for use in preventing suicide or in reducing suicidal thoughts or actions. SPRAVATO® is not for use in place of hospitalization if your healthcare provider determines that hospitalization is needed, even if improvement is experienced after the first dose of SPRAVATO®. SPRAVATO® is not for use as a medicine to prevent or relieve pain (anesthetic). It is not known if SPRAVATO® is safe or effective as an anesthetic medicine. It is not known if SPRAVATO® is safe and effective in children. (Please see additional Important Safety Information including Boxed WARNINGS, limitations of use, and a list of side effects below. Click here to learn more.)

SPRAVATO is only available through a restricted distribution program called the SPRAVATO Risk Evaluation & Mitigation Strategy (REMS). SPRAVATO can only be administered at a certified healthcare setting, and patients self-administer the pre-filled nasal device at a REMS-certified treatment center under direct clinical supervision and are monitored for at least two hours after taking SPRAVATO. SPRAVATO may have serious side effects such as sedation, dissociation, and respiratory depression, and the risk of abuse and misuse.

SPRAVATO represents a different treatment approach for TRD. Unlike traditional antidepressants that work on serotonin, norepinephrine and dopamine, SPRAVATO acts on glutamate, a chemical messenger in the brain that is thought to regulate depression. The role of glutamate in depression and the exact way SPRAVATO works are unknown.

As his depressive symptoms improved, Jeremiah began to engage more with others. He also joined a support group for Black men navigating these challenges. Hearing other people’s stories reminds him that he’s not alone. Today, he works as an IT and cybersecurity instructor in Chicago, speaks at industry conferences, and builds robots in his spare time.

Jeremiah’s experience is his own, and treatment decisions are personal. “There’s no one treatment that’s right for everybody,” Dr. Chepke says. In his practice, Dr. Chepke has witnessed reductions in certain patients’ depressive symptoms when incorporating SPRAVATO into their treatment. While not all of his patients may benefit, seeing some move from repeatedly cycling through different treatments to an option studied specifically for TRD has helped shape how he approaches care for this population.

If you haven’t found relief from your depressive symptoms, talk with your doctor about the options that may be appropriate for you—and most importantly, know that there is hope.

Jeremiah and Dr. Chepke were compensated for their time participating in this article.

#4846. Billy Joel at Home: 10 Photos of the Piano Man Through the Decades

For Billy Joel, New York is more than just a place. It’s an inextricable part of what makes the singer who he is. “My speech patterns are New York. The music that I like, it was all New York–based. That’s what I think of when I think of home,” he said in his 2025 HBO documentary Billy Joel: And So It Goes. “It’s my roots.”

The Bronx native grew up in Hicksville, a middle-class suburb of Nassau County on Long Island. His family struggled to make ends meet. “There was poor, and then there was Billy Joel poor. He was lucky if he had enough money to buy a pack of cigarettes,” his childhood friend and fellow musician Jon Small said in And So It Goes. According to Joel’s sister Judy, no matter how hard times were, their mother Rosalind insisted he take piano lessons. His talent “had to be nurtured,” Judy said in the HBO doc. “She knew that he was going to be something someday.”

Before he indeed became something, Joel worked on an oyster boat. “I used to look up at this mansion on the hill and wonder what it would be like to live in a house like that,” he said in the documentary, referencing the waterfront property on Centre Island he nicknamed MiddleSea. “I used to think, ‘They’re rich bastards. They never had to work a day in their life.’ Well, I own that house now. It’s not finished yet. And neither am I.”

Read on for a glimpse into the Grammy winner’s life, from his early days in New York to his brief stint in Los Angeles and return home.

Joel’s music career took the Long Island native to Los Angeles in the early 1970s, and he signed with Columbia Records in 1973. After three years in LA, he and his first wife, Elizabeth Weber, returned to his home state, where he completed his fourth studio album, Turnstiles. “I wanted to get back to New York and make more of a rock and roll album,” Joel explained in And So It Goes. “I was on a bus on my way back to Highland Falls, New York. Elizabeth found us a house up on the Hudson River, and it was fall. It was just gorgeous. The colors were ablaze, the trees were, like, gold and red, and I remember thinking, ‘This is the New York State that I loved when I was a kid. This is magic. We don’t have this in California.’ And I wrote this love song to New York on the bus.” It would become “New York State of Mind,” one of Joel’s most popular tunes.

The singer-songwriter poses with some of his records in January 1978.

Joel’s fifth studio album, 1977’s The Stranger, was a runaway success—but the singer, pictured alongside his accolades in New York in 1978, told Playboy a few years later that his newfound fortune didn’t faze him. “I read these stories about Peter Frampton’s multimillion-dollar mansion, 15 Rolls-Royces and all that,” he said. “Who cares? It’s all bullshit. What was his last record like? Was it any good? That’s the question. People get hung up on the money thing. It’s nice to have four motorcycles. It’s fun. And I walk into the garage and go, ‘Holy shit! I’ve got four motorcycles!’ But I don’t go beyond a certain point.”

Joel, his then-wife Elizabeth, and their dog in 1978.

Instead of splurging on a million-dollar mansion, Joel told Playboy that when he and his wife decided to buy a home, “We got a $300,000 house with a mortgage like everybody else.” Their glass house, featuring floor-to-ceiling windows overlooking the Long Island Sound, was located in the town of Oyster Bay on Long Island’s North Shore. Joel appears poised to hurl a rock at the home on the cover of his 1980 album, Glass Houses. “The old thing about people who live in glass houses shouldn’t throw stones—I don’t believe it,” he said. “I think, Why not? Take chances. I really wanted to throw a rock at my own house.”

Joel and Elizabeth at their Long Island residence.

In the 1970s, Joel asked Weber to be his manager. “The company I’m with now is New York–based,” Joel said of his representation. “It’s called Home Run—nothing to do with baseball. It’s a home-run agency.” Weber got right to work. She recalled in his HBO documentary that the “story [Joel] likes to tell” of her early days on the job is that he woke up the next morning to phones everywhere and “cabinets installed.” However, she said, “That’s not really true, but it’s close to true.” The couple (seen here at Joel’s grand piano in their living room) split time between their Manhattan apartment, where they worked, and Oyster Bay. Weber left her role managing Joel when the two split, and her brother Frank picked up where she left off. Home Run dissolved amid financial woes in the ’80s, and Joel eventually pressed charges against Frank over mishandled funds; the parties reached a settlement, the terms of which have not been disclosed publicly.

The musician mixing tapes in the music studio of his New York home.

The Oyster Bay house, a midcentury-modern residence, was not far from where Joel grew up in Hicksville. Photographed here in his at-home music studio in 1978, the singer’s career was on the upswing—but his relationship with Weber was growing tense. “Having a big boom in record success, I think my marriage was starting to unravel around then; 1979, it wasn’t the happiest time,” Joel once said. “Record success doesn’t translate into happiness.” Joel assumed things were paying off financially, but he admitted he “wasn’t aware” how much money he was actually bringing in. “I know we were living in a nice house, my wife was going out and buying all kinds of nice stuff,” he said. “I never really went out and did that.”

Joel multitasks in his LA home studio in 1984.

Though Joel had settled down on the East Coast, he told the Los Angeles Times that his California years cross his mind “all the time.” The singer, pictured here in LA in 1984, wrote his hit song “Piano Man” based on his experience as a lounge musician (using the name Bill Martin) at a now-defunct bar near the corner of Wilshire Boulevard and Western Avenue during the early 1970s. “I wonder what happened to the people I knew—the people in the bar in ‘Piano Man,’” he said. “It was the Executive Room in the Wilshire district. I got tips and made union scale, and I was able to afford an apartment in Studio City. The weather was great; the people were nice.”

Though it appears Joel lived like a rock star in Los Angeles—as seen here in 1984, perched on a sheepskin-style throw over a leather sofa with a pack of Marlboros and a landline telephone by his side—he told the Los Angeles Times in 2023 that he felt more like “an exiled writer living in Paris” during his early stint in the City of Angels. “I went from being an insignificant nobody to the Piano Man while I was there,” he said. “I still look back to my time in LA with a certain amount of romance.”

Joel is pictured here at the dinner table in 2001. When The New Yorker paid him a visit at his Centre Island residence in 2014, he described the interior’s aesthetic as “Catholic martyrs and saints, grotesqueries.” In the library, Joel—who decorated the place himself—had a model of the Queen Mary on his mantel, and in the living room facing the fireplace was a triptych of the Last Supper along with silver jugs and bowls on a nearby table.

Joel’s various properties have passed through some famous hands. He and his second wife, supermodel Christie Brinkley, owned a 12-acre oceanfront property in the East Hampton hamlet of Amagansett. The couple raised daughter Alexa Ray Joel in the Long Island dwelling. It was later sold to Jerry and Jessica Seinfeld for $32 million. According to The New Yorker, Joel also sold a duplex on Central Park West to singer-songwriter Sting for $5 million and a house on Martha’s Vineyard to businessman Mickey Drexler. At one point, Joel purchased a home in the Hamptons from Jaws star Roy Scheider.

“As a little kid, I always liked boats and the romance of living on an island,” Joel told Parade in 2018. The singer—pictured here on an East Hampton dock in 2001—has always felt at home on the water. In 2007 he designed a 57-foot powerboat called the Vendetta that can go about 50 knots, per The New Yorker. Boating represented “freedom,” Joel said in his documentary. “I am the captain of my ship.”

#4844. Seattle plans 200 curbside EV charging stations – and you can request one

Seattle plans to add up to 200 public curbside Level 2 EV charging stations by 2030, and residents can now request one near their home or apartment.

For apartment dwellers and anyone who parks on the street, that’s a useful alternative to making a separate trip to charge. More than half of Seattle’s homes are apartments or condos, according to City Light. Older houses and houseboats can also lack somewhere to plug in off the street.

Seattle City Light and the Seattle Department of Transportation are targeting neighborhoods with the fewest charging options.

The chargers are intended for topping up while parked near home. Seattle says its Level 2 curbside EV charging stations can add around 12–30 miles of range per hour, depending on the vehicle and equipment. All the new locations will be open to the public.

City Light currently charges $0.21 per kilowatt-hour at its Level 2 chargers. At that rate, adding 30 kWh would cost $6.30. Using the utility’s estimate of about 3 miles per kWh, that’s roughly 90 miles of range, depending on the EV and driving conditions.

The expansion follows a 2023–2024 pilot at 31 locations, which SDOT says drew strong use and positive community feedback. Seattle’s installations will be funded by the transportation levy voters approved in 2024.

Residents can request a curbside charger through City Light’s program page. Applications will remain open through fall 2027, with locations reviewed and selected on an ongoing basis. The city will consider charging gaps, environmental and equity goals, and whether a site has the electrical infrastructure needed for installation.

#4842. What Rest-Pause Training Can Do for Your Workout

A simple practice lets you push past failure—without lowering the weight.

TRY AS YOU might, you can’t pump out reps forever when you’re working toward building bigger muscles. Eventually, you‘ll be too fatigued to complete another rep with good form, a point referred to as “technical failure.” Pushing beyond your last good rep can lead to sloppy lifting mechanics, which can compromise your results or, worse increase your risk of injury. If you find yourself stuck lifting the same weight for the same reps, it may be time to get creative with how you push past that iron hurdle.

One way to head off the siren song of ego lifting is by implementing a planned rest-pause set. It’s an intense lifting technique that requires focus and intention, and as effective as it can be, it shouldn’t be done for every set or even every exercise.

By briefly resting after reaching failure, you can squeeze out a few more quality reps using the same weight. A few extra reps might not seem like a big deal, but they can add up over time, giving your muscles an extra dose of the tension that drives growth.

To do a rest-pause set, you’ll take an exercise to the point where you can’t complete another rep with good form. You’ll then rest for five to 15 seconds—in one MH workout plan, fitness director Ebenezer Samuel, C.S.C.S. recommends taking “three deep breaths” for a pause—then squeeze out a few more reps (expect to be able to do two to four) using the same weight. You can repeat this process, though one additional round of reps is a good starting point.

If you rest longer than 20 seconds, Alexander Rothstein, an exercise physiologist and program coordinator of exercise science at the New York Institute of Technology, says you’re starting to approach a standard rest interval. "If you give yourself that brief moment to… recover, and then you continue the set, you haven't flushed away all of the waste products, and you haven't fully recovered your energy stores, but you are still capable of doing a few more high-quality reps,” he explains.

The purpose of a rest-pause set is to push your muscle to complete a few more hard (but high-quality) reps. If you’re aiming to build muscle, it’s those hard reps near the end of a set that are key; a rest-pause set allows you to sneak in a few more of those reps. While lifters of any experience level can perform rest-pause sets, they’re especially useful for advanced lifters who’ve already cashed in their newbie gains and find it increasingly difficult to progress their lifts and add muscle.

Say you’re doing the dumbbell bench press, an exercise on which you’ve been stuck using the same 50-pound dumbbells for sets of 8 to 10 reps for over a month. You get to that 10th rep and, once again, can’t muster another. Instead of calling it this time, you’ll sit up, rest the dumbbells on your thighs for 15 seconds, and then bust out another two reps. Congrats. You just eked out more worthwhile reps, which, over time, should help you progress.

“But isn’t that cheating?” you ask. No—and even if it were, there are times when cheating pays off for muscle gains. And research suggests that traditional sets and rest-pause sets can produce similar gains in strength and muscle. One small study had 18 experienced lifters perform six weeks of traditional sets or rest-pause training with the same relative load. One group completed three sets of six reps; the other did one set to failure and then as many rest-pause sets as necessary to hit 18 reps. Both groups achieved similar strength gains, but the rest-pause group experienced greater increases in thigh muscle thickness and leg-press muscular endurance.

As for how to start using them, pick one exercise per workout—ideally, a move you’re struggling to progress—and do the final set of that exercise as a rest-pause set. This often works best with the final exercise in your workout. The rest-pause protocol can be downright exhausting, and using them too early may compromise your ability to hit your typical reps and weights during subsequent sets.

One note: You can perform rest-pause sets with just about any exercise, but there are two places where they’re especially beneficial. Weight machines are the safest, letting you easily push to fatigue, then take your brief “rest”. Exercises that offer support for stabilizing muscles (think: chest-supported rows) also work well. And many single-joint free-weight exercises, like dumbbell curls are good options. If you’re going to attempt a rest-pause set with the bench press or back squat, have a good spotter on hand.

There’s more than one way to increase the volume of a single set, and these methods are often referred to as intensity techniques. Below, we’ll briefly compare the three most popular ones to rest-pause sets.

A drop set is when you reach failure on a lift, then immediately reduce the load (often by 10 to 20 percent) and try to squeeze out a few more reps. In many ways, it’s similar to a rest-pause set, but because you’re lightening the weight, you’ll find it easier to maintain good form.

“Personally, I just like the volume approach of drop sets,” Rothstein says. "When you do drop sets, obviously the load is being reduced, so it's not as potentially strength beneficial as it might be to just do rest-pauses and still lift heavy loads."

A cluster set is when you break up a traditional straight set into a series of mini sets, or clusters, with short rest periods between each. They're a popular training method among strength athletes, such as powerlifters and weightlifters, who want to accumulate more total tonnage.

Say, for example, you can typically deadlift 250 pounds for eight reps. You could load 285 to 300 pounds on the bar and perform four two-rep clusters, resting 15 to 30 seconds between, to complete the same eight reps with roughly 15 to 20 percent more weight.

The main difference between rest-pause and cluster sets is that cluster sets strategically use rest to achieve a preplanned number of reps, often at a higher weight. Rest-pause sets have you take a few breaths after reaching failure to push past what you can normally do rep-wise. Cluster sets are likely superior to rest-pause sets for building strength.

Instead of resting and then doing more reps once you reach failure, you can perform forced reps, where your spotter provides just enough assistance to help you complete a few more reps with good form. Forced reps are usually done on exercises where a spotter can easily help; think the bench press or certain machine exercises, not deadlifts or heavy back squats.

While you’re technically pushing past failure, you don’t have control over how much assistance your spotter provides; this can vary from workout to workout or even rep to rep. You can, however, control the eccentric portion of the contraction after the spotter has helped you, so if you’re doing forced reps, it’s a must to lower the weight slowly to get the most from these. Forced reps can be a useful occasional technique if you have an experienced spotter who knows how much assistance to provide; because they’re forcing you to acclimate to increased time-under-tension with a weight that you know is challenging.

BYD will open pre-orders for the Denza N8 EV next week, a large five-seat luxury electric SUV with a CLTC range of over 623 miles (1,000 km).

The Denza N8 initially went on sale in China in 2023 as a mid-to-large-size luxury SUV. It was available as a plug-in hybrid (PHEV) with six- and seven-seat configurations.

BYD is preparing to introduce an all-electric version that will deliver the same electric-only driving range as the PHEV did on a full charge and full tank of gas, combined.

“The king of large 5-seater pure electric vehicles,” as Denza calls it, will use BYD’s second-generation Blade Batteries and Flash Charging Technology. The setup delivers “a world-leading 1,003 km pure electric range,” under CLTC conditions, Denza claimed.

BYD’s 1,500 kW Flash Charging tech powers compatible vehicles from 10% to 70% in just five minutes. To go from 10% to 97%, it takes only nine minutes.

Li Hui, Denza’s general manager, announced on Weibo on October 22 that the company plans to open pre-orders for the Denza N8 EV on October 26, with the official launch in November.

Update 10/26/2026: BYD opens pre-orders for the new Denza N8 EV (read more here).

According to a regulatory filing released by China’s Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT) in August, the Denza N8 EV is 5,150 mm long, 1,999 mm wide, and 1,820 mm high, with a 3,075 mm wheelbase.

The Denza N8 EV will use a massive 130.15 kWh battery, providing a pure electric CLTC range of up to 623 miles (1,003 km).

BYD will offer a single rear-wheel-drive (RWD) or a tri-motor all-wheel-drive (AWD) powertrain. The RWD version uses a single motor producing either 320 kW (429 hp) or 370 kW (496 hp).

The tri-motor Denza N8, meanwhile, is based on BYD’s e3 platform. The setup includes a 270 kW (362 hp) front motor and two 310 kW (416 hp) rear motors, delivering a combined output of 890 kW (1,193 hp).

Inside, the luxury SUV features two huge digital screens. One 30″ center infotainment screen spans nearly the entire passenger-side dashboard, and a new 43″ (1.1 meter) panoramic head-up display (PHUD) sits below the windshield.

Like many new BYD models, the cabin adopts a minimalist design with premium features like ambient lighting, a three-spoke steering wheel, and higher-end materials.

Ahead of its official launch, the Denza N8 EV was spotted in China undisguised. New images from Autohome show the luxury SUV driving in public, with roof-mounted LiDAR and a sleek, premium look.

Last month, BYD also launched the Denza N8L EV, a slightly longer six-seat version of the current PHEV sold in China.

The Denza N8L EV is available in two versions. The N8L EV Premium starts at 299,800 yuan, or about $45,000, while the Flagship model is priced from 329,800 yuan ($49,000).

Seems Byd launches a new model every month, almost feels like early 2000s GM with 70+ models.

Both versions use a 130.15 kWh BYD Blade Battery 2.0, providing a CLTC range of up to 596 miles (960 km).

The N8L EV is 5,200 mm long, 1,999 mm wide, and 1,820 mm high, with a 3,075 mm wheelbase, or slightly longer than the standard version. It’s about the same size as the current PHEV. The larger SUV features a “208L super-large intelligent electric front trunk.”

BYD will open pre-orders for the Denza N8 EV on October 26, followed by an official launch in November. Check back soon for prices and more details.

When I think of Anthropologie, I think of its versatile wardrobe staples like denim, office-appropriate blouses, and midi-length dresses. However, I was only recently introduced to its newest label, Daily Practice, which launched in summer 2024. The laid-back loungewear line combines style, comfort, and versatility for busy women who do it all.

Daily Practice is Anthropologie’s loungewear label, offering styles for everything from downtime to playtime to working at home. It’s less “activewear” and more “cozy athleisure” meant to multitask in our everyday lives. Think: sherpa fleeces, sweats, puffer jackets, casual tees, and stretchy dresses.

Ahead of Daily Practice’s latest collection, Anthropologie reached out to Women’s Health to try some pieces from the launch. Over the past two weeks, I tested four styles: a fleece quarter-zip, balloon-style joggers, a mock neck pullover sweater, and straight-leg sweatpants. Since New York is having transitional fall weather, I wore each piece on its own and layered with base layers like T-shirts and long sleeves. I also wore some styles while working from home, at the movie theater, and spectating at the New York City Marathon.

Of everything in the new collection, I was most excited to try this quarter-zip sherpa jacket. A fleece is one of the best layers to have in your fall and winter wardrobe. These laid-back pants look just as good styled with ballet flats and a cardigan as they do lounging on my couch. The lightweight, breathable cotton material has just enough spandex to make the joggers feel buttery smooth against the skin. Note: The pants are fairly thin, so they’re not suitable for freezing temps, but since they’re baggy, you can easily layer leggings or thermal underwear underneath.

I prefer the Ease State Pants when I’m working from home and don’t want to feel like I’m sitting in sweats all day. They’re also great for light movement like yoga, walking, or running errands. I’d suggest taking your normal size in these pants for that balloon-leg look—the drawstring waist will ensure a perfect fit.

Designed with a relaxed silhouette and a ribbed mock neck, this cotton-blend knit pullover feels like a sweatshirt but looks much more put together. I love the dropped shoulders for an easygoing look you can dress up or down. Contrasting ribbed trim along the sleeves and cuffs adds style and stretch.

This style definitely runs large (I ordered a size small), and I found excessive fabric around the bottom of the torso that didn’t drape the way I wanted. However, as a tall person with long arms, I appreciate the sleeve length. The mock neck is also comfortable to wear all day without itching or feeling tight.

My only complaint is that the waist runs very large. I wish there was a drawstring or more elastic in the waistband because they’re too large to stay up on my hips. I do like the low-rise style, which offers a more trendy look that’s great for layering, but I would size down next time. For now, I haven’t worn them out of the house since they’re too big, but they’ll be great for layering over bike shorts or thermal leggings this winter.

Daily Practice knows its audience: working women, multi-tasking moms, stylish consumers who care about looking cute and feeling comfy. Whether I’m at home watching a movie or on the go, I know I’ll reach for these versatile pieces a lot over the next couple of months. Similar to Anthropologie’s other in-house labels, Daily Practice runs large. So if you’re between sizes, I would recommend sizing down.

#4835. Matt Damon and David Letterman Pop into The Gilded Age Just for Funzies

HBO’s period drama got a very modern surprise from two very recognizable faces.

IF YOU’RE NOT familiar with HBO’s The Gilded Age, it’s a pretty easy show to explain. Set in New York City during the titular era—the rapidly changing 1880s—the show is an exploration of the rich-people trials and tribulations of a new money family (led by Carrie Coon and Morgan “Train Daddy” Spector) and their neighbors, an old money family (led by Christine Baranski).

One of the show’s most important aspects is its production design, with intricately built sets and elaborately planned costumes helping to transport its viewers back nearly 150 years. Immersion is the name of the game.

With a setup like that, The Gilded Age is just about the last show where you’d expect to see a couple of our most recognizable modern stars walk directly across the screen—but that’s just what Matt Damon and David Letterman did, less than 10 minutes into the show’s season 4 premiere.

Damon, the Oscar-winning movie star who earlier this year led Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey and Netflix’s The Rip, and Letterman, the legendary talk show host, walked across the screen in full costume, saying nothing, in a blink-and-you’ll-miss-it moment.

As it turns out, according to a story published by Vulture, the whole thing was born from Letterman’s lifelong desire to make a surprise appearance in something as a background actor, something that began way back in 1977 when he saw a fellow comedian friend slyly appear in the background of a scene in Annie Hall.

In recent years, Letterman has apparently come close to shooting background scenes in Wes Anderson’s The Phoenician Scheme, the upcoming Michael B. Jordan-directed version of The Thomas Crown Affair, and Black Rabbit alongside Jason Bateman—but for one reason or another, none of them came to be.

Letterman filmed an upcoming episode of his current show, the Netflix interview series My Next Guest Needs No Introduction with David Letterman, with Damon, and discovered that Damon and Ben Affleck began their careers as background actors, and, for the sake of the bit, figured this would be the perfect opportunity to see his dream come to fruition. “We thought, Okay, this could be the perfect opportunity,” Next Guest showrunner Isabel Richardson explained to Vulture. “It’d be really fun for Dave to do this with Academy Award–winner Matt Damon, and it tied into his origin story really well.”

Damon, luckily, was into the idea too—and they made it happen. “It was a kind of hysterical moment when our production supervisor Leah Baker came up to me on set and was like, ‘Well, I have a kind of funny, interesting question: Would you like Dave Letterman and Matt Damon to be background on our set one day?’” Gilded Age showrunner Churchill said in the same Vulture story. “I just started laughing.”

Surprise appearances and cameos have long been a part of Damon’s playbook. Marvel fans certainly remember his brief appearances in movies like Deadpool 2 and Thor: Ragnarok, while fans of Damon’s frequent collaborator Steven Soderbergh’s movies won’t forget his surprise turns in movies like No Sudden Move and Che: Part Two. He even appeared in a very brief role in Ethan Coen’s Drive Away Dolls after working with Ethan and his brother Joel on the 2010 hit True Grit.

Perhaps Damon’s most memorable (and truly most random) cameo comes in the 2004 comedy Eurotrip, though. He appears early in the film as Donnie, the lead singer of an alt-rock band who sings a song about the affair he was apparently having with the main character’s girlfriend. “Scotty Doesn’t Know” is a pillar of both 2000s pop-punk and that era’s teen sex comedy movement, and Damon’s completely out-of-nowhere cameo is a huge reason why.

And, look, HBO seems to enjoy this kind of thing anyway. Just last month, we spotted the University of Nebraska’s head football coach Matt Rhule in the final episode of Lanterns. Does his appearance make sense in a show set in Nebraska? Sure. Did we ever expect to see Matt Rhule in an acclaimed, highly watched HBO drama set in a superhero world? No, we certainly did not.

It’s fun (and probably a bit trippy at first) to come to grips with seeing who you think you’re seeing. And if, somehow, you don’t know who either of those two are, you probably won’t notice at all and won’t think a thing. And isn’t that how all great cameos should go, really?

#4834. The World’s Most Famous Architects Are Building in Albania. I Had to Find Out Why

“I'll try to focus on this, which is not the easiest thing today,” says Edi Rama, the embattled prime minister of Albania, after a night spent monitoring violent protests in the capital, Tirana. But Rama quickly warms to one of his favorite subjects. “Architecture,” he says, choosing his words carefully, “has the power to change societies. It’s like a strong medicine. It can heal, or it can kill.”

A journalist who covers architecture, I had been hearing about a building boom in Albania for several years. It seemed like half the architects I knew in New York were on a first-name basis with the prime minister, a working artist and, at 6’-7”, a former pro basketball player. So on October 19 I flew to Tirana—a short side-trip from Greece, where I was on vacation with my husband—to look at some of the new buildings and interview Rama about them. But I arrived during a season of civil unrest. The prime minister, whose assistant had told I needn’t postpone the trip because everything was fine, had moved to a secure location on the outskirts of the city; some of the buildings I had come to see had just been vandalized by protesters; and at one point I was accused, publicly, of aiding a government spy. (The charge was— need I even say this—absurd.) And, because I’m in the early stages of Parkinson’s disease, I experienced all this from a four-wheeled mobility scooter, which I had rented for about $100.

As I tooled around the city center, much of it seemed unaffected by the protests. In fact, most of Tirana was charming. But weren’t those Molotov cocktails we heard going off during an al fresco dinner? Those weren’t on my drinks menu.

What was on my menu in Tirana, a city of about 600,000 in a country of about 2.3 million, was confusion. Confusion about why the protesters were so angry, and about why the prime minister seemed so unconcerned. In his 13 years in office, Rama, 62, has been remaking as much of Albania as possible with the help of foreign architects. Even the heavily guarded villa where he agreed to be interviewed, a raw concrete building dyed bright red, is largely the work of the Spanish architect Pablo Bofill.

When protesters began demanding Rama’s resignation last May, he was about to host his second annual gathering of architects from around the world, one of the high points of his year. Architects like the Danish superstar Bjarke Ingels and the Chilean Alejandro Aravena, who won the Pritzker Prize in 2016, “pay to come here and talk and they love it,” Rama says. But this year the get-together, from June 3 to 5, drew protesters with signs that read “Starchitects go home!” Those protests presaged the more violent demonstrations in October and November.

I haven’t attended either of Rama’s conclaves, but what I’ve heard reminds me of my visit to Ordos, Inner Mongolia, in 2008, which I wrote about for The New York Times. A wealthy industrialist, aided by the artist Ai Weiwei, had brought 100 young architects from around the world to the isolated desert city. Their task was to design 100 villas for anonymous (and seemingly nonexistent) Chinese millionaires. The architects picked numbers out of a bowl to determine which of the 100 sites was theirs, and before flying home they were paid for their designs with wads of cash. None of the villas was built, but being in Ordos was a bonding experience for a generation of architects, a few of whom have recently been to Tirana. At least until the latest protests, the mood among Rama-anointed architects—giddy optimism coupled with uncertainty about what would actually be built—echoed the mood in Ordos almost 20 years ago. Both situations felt surreal.

Rama normally works in an office on the Boulevard of Martyrs of the Nation in the center of Tirana. But on October 20 the boulevard's sidewalks were missing hundreds of paving stones, which protesters had used to shatter storefronts. (Some that weren’t shattered bore hastily made signs telling protesters, “Don’t target us. We are with you.”) And some of the stones were reportedly thrown at police during nighttime clashes that authorities say left hundreds injured. Police have used tear gas and rubber bullets as protesters set small buildings, like an information kiosk in the vast Skanderbeg Square, on fire. Near the shell of the kiosk, workers scrubbed fresh graffiti off a statue of Skanderbeg himself.

The Tirana Pyramid, built by followers of the brutal dictator Enver Hoxha, who died in 1985, as his memorial, and turned into a public amenity by the Rotterdam firm MVRDV, was also damaged.

There’s a reason some Albanians—it’s impossible to say how many—resent the foreign architects and the attention lavished on them. In the 26 years since he became the mayor of Tirana and then prime minister, Rama has initiated or encouraged more than 50 international architecture competitions for projects ranging from parks to museums to large housing developments. Forty-eight of those were won by foreign architects (some working with Albanian firms), according to Adelina Greca, who leads the National Territorial Planning Agency, which organizes competitions for the government. Only two were won by Albanian firms working alone. In addition, Rama has played matchmaker, giving private developers the names of foreign architects he strongly recommends they hire.

As a result, Tirana’s compact city center is filled with buildings in bright colors and novel shapes. There is a so-called vertical forest, a skyscraper laden with trees and shrubs, by the Italian architect Stefano Boeri. The green-colored building is just a stone’s throw from the bright red Marriott by another Italian architect, Marco Casamonti. The Plaza Hotel, by architect Johan Anrys, of the Belgian firm 51N4E, starts as an ellipse at its base and morphs into a rectangle at its crown. But the champion attention-getter is a condo building by MVRDV in the shape of a head. Its facade and balconies resolve into facial features, most conspicuously a pronounced nose. The architects have publicly identified it as the head of Skanderbeg, a 15th century military hero. But some Albanians think it’s Rama. Both ideas are “urban legends,” says the prime minister. “It’s the form of a man through history,” he says, contradicting the architects’ own statement. Nodding at this reporter, he says, “It also looks like you."

Tirana's Rock (aka the Skandebeg building) is an MVRDV-designed condo in the shape of a head

A Marriott designed by Marco Casamonti of Archea Associati, left, and the “vertical forest” skyscraper by Stefano Boeri

The vertical forest, the Marriott and the Plaza Hotel are all handsome additions to the city. So, too, is the “head,” but is it too much of an architectural one-liner? Who, I wonder as I pass it several times a day, is going to want to live in the nose?

Rama tells me—on-the-record and perhaps unwisely—that the only Albanian architects who have a problem with his overtures to foreign firms are “the mediocre ones.”

Anrys, who 22 years ago became one of the first foreign architects in Albania, told me that working there has taught him "what architecture truly means for improving society.” He said he knows that Albanian architects wonder, "Are we not good enough?" and believe we're taking jobs from them. "It isn't true. I have a studio in Tirana with 20 Albanian architects." Overall he says, the foreign architects have “brought Albanian architects more work than we've taken."

Rama tells me—on-the-record and perhaps unwisely—that the only Albanian architects who have a problem with his overtures to foreign firms are “the mediocre ones.” The rest, he explains, see that having first-rate architects from abroad, including Herzog & de Meuron, OMA, and Diller Scofidio & Renfro, working in Albania will raise everyone’s game.

Rama tells me—on-the-record and perhaps unwisely—that the only Albanian architects who have a problem with his overtures to foreign firms are “the mediocre ones.”

The foreign architects who win competitions are required to enlist architects licensed in Albania to help them execute their plans. Rama compares the situation to that of China, which 20 years ago was giving its most prominent building commissions to foreign architects, including some of the same ones working in Albania today. Chinese architects, Rama says, got a free education from the western masters.

“If we continue this kind of cooperation,” says Greca, who has worked for Rama almost continuously since 2003, “there will come a day when Albanian architects will win competitions not only here but around the world.”

Anti-government protesters on the streets of Tirana, with the art installation Tirana Moons by Austrian architect Chris Precht in the background

But Greca’s association with Rama has made her a controversial figure among local architects. On my first day in town, our route intersects that of a lunchtime protest march. We stop to watch. Greca notices many architects and architecture students in the crowd. (The Faculty of Architecture and Urbanism of the Polytechnic University of Tirana is nearby.)

Within minutes, Gent Progni, an organizer of the march, posts a photo of Greca and me on Instagram. The caption claims she had sunk so low as to use a disabled person (me) as cover to spy on the marchers. (Ten days later, the post has almost 7,000 “likes.”) Later, in a text responding to questions from this reporter, Progni wrote:

“My opposition is not to foreign architects but to the way Edi Rama uses prestigious international names to legitimize controversial development projects, often without transparency, meaningful public consultation, or accountability. This is a significant issue for our protest movement, but it is part of a much larger struggle against corruption, the concentration of power, and the sale of Albania’s public wealth.”

Rama himself isn’t happy with all of the new buildings in Tirana. He complained about one whose facades are made of stone “until a certain altitude,” where the cost-cutting developer switched to a printed material that only looks like stone. Other buildings stand partially complete, or complete but eerily empty. And in several cases developers have replaced foreign architects with local ones midstream, in order to complete buildings without meeting the original design specifications. “We need the investors to stick with the architects,” Rama says. But funding is less available than he would like. “Certain architecture needs a certain quality,” he says, philosophically. “But compromises are forced by the limitations of the place.”

The problems with his building boom go deeper than facade materials. There are accusations of money laundering and other forms of corruption, which grew louder at the end of May, when Rama agreed to support efforts by a company associated with Jared Kushner and Ivanka Trump to build luxury resorts on previously undeveloped land. It was a coincidence that the big architecture conference started just a few days later, leading directly to the calls for starchitects to scram. Among the protesters, that demand became entangled with environmental and anti-Trump sentiments in what became known as the Flamingo Revolution.

A housing project by Madrid-based firm SelgasCano

European journalist and curator Anneke Abhelakh has recently published a brilliantly illuminating book, The Albanian Files, which gives 60 foreign architecture firms eight or more pages to describe the work they are doing in Albania. Altogether, the book lists more than 500 projects. Of those, only about one-tenth have been realized. Rama says he is looking forward to the completion of many more.

But can that really happen, given the pressure to resign? The prime minister, who won the most recent election by the biggest majority of his career, says he isn’t going anywhere.

In fact, seemingly oblivious to the mood on the street, he wants to further celebrate his stable of foreign architects. Near the end of my half-hour interview, he mentions that he is thinking of turning The Albanian Files into a museum, with one room for each of the 60 foreign firms to show drawings, models and photographs of their work. He said he already has a site for what he says will be “a big store of dreams, hopes and challenges, illusions and delusions. It will be a great place to go.” Its designer will be chosen, naturally, in an international architectural competition.

I left Albania with lots of questions and thousands of photos to sort through. In one of them I have my arm around Rama. Why the affectionate pose? A reflex when the camera comes out. But I suppose also that, politics aside, I can’t hate a man who loves architecture.

Prime Minster Rama with writer Fred Bernstein

#4831. Tesla skipped the most important shareholder question on its earnings call

Tesla skipped one of its top shareholder questions on its Q3 2026 earnings call: when Hardware 3 owners will find out if they get a free computer upgrade for the unsupervised “Full Self-Driving” they paid for.

The question ranked fifth by shares on Say. Tesla read and answered questions ranked below it. It went past this one without a word.

Tesla takes retail shareholder questions through the Say platform before every earnings call, and shareholders upvote them with their shares. When we previewed the Q3 2026 earnings as submissions closed, the HW3 question sat fifth with 557 votes and 652,900 shares.

“Tesla has acknowledged that HW3 vehicles cannot support unsupervised FSD. When will owners know whether they can upgrade their hardware for free, and when will Tesla provide a clear plan?”

Head of investor relations Travis Axelrod read nine Say questions on Wednesday’s call. Tesla answered the Cybercab scaling question, unsupervised FSD in customer cars, Cybercab ownership, and robotaxi and Optimus unit economics. Then it went on to questions about Optimus training data, Optimus revenue, FSD mapping, and factory production rates.

The Optimus revenue and FSD mapping questions both ranked below HW3 in every ranking published before the call. The Optimus training data one didn’t even make the top 10.

Axelrod closed the segment with “That’s it for the Say.com questions.” No analyst asked about HW3 either, and HW3, AI3, or a retrofit didn’t come up once during the entire call.

The second question Tesla took was “When can we anticipate FSD unsupervised in customer cars?”

Ashok Elluswamy, Tesla’s head of AI, answered that the same software running in Model Y robotaxis and the Cybercab will come to customers with FSD v15, and that “somewhere around Q2 next year” the first customer vehicles could join the Robotaxi fleet.

That’s another delay, a new timeline that history suggests will likely be pushed back, and an HW4 answer. Musk admitted on the Q1 2026 call that “Hardware 3 simply does not have the capability to achieve unsupervised FSD,” citing an eighth of HW4’s memory bandwidth. So every time Tesla gives a date for unsupervised FSD, it’s a date that doesn’t apply to millions of cars Tesla sold as having all the hardware needed for full self-driving.

And HW3 owners have been promised something by Musk on each of the last two calls. In April, he talked about “microfactories” in major cities to swap computers and cameras, and a discounted trade-in. In July, when a Truist analyst asked about it, Musk said upgrading would make sense “at some point” and floated skipping HW4 for a next-gen board or AI5, which goes to Optimus first.

No cost, no timeline, no process. And this quarter, not even a mention.

Tesla sold FSD for up to $15,000 on the promise that its cars already had the hardware. Now it’s facing class actions in the US, China, and Australia, and a Dutch collective claim that grew to nearly 7,000 HW3 owners with a law firm behind it. Documents from Dutch regulator RDW show Tesla only submitted HW4 for FSD approval in Europe.

HW3 owners got a stripped-down FSD v14 “Lite” this year. It’s a supervised driver assist, and it doesn’t come close to what they bought.

We don’t think this was an accident. Tesla picks which Say questions it reads and in what order, and it chose to answer a question about Optimus revenue it said it had “kind of already answered” over one backed by 650,000 shares about the product its customers already paid for.

Of course they will avoid the question so they can delay this as long as possible and hope the existing owners will just give up or the cars will just work themselves out of the market with write offs over time. That is a lot of money Tesla would have to spend to upgrade the HW that they never intend to.

Any answer Tesla gives on HW3 has a dollar figure attached, and it’s probably a big one: replacing the computer and cameras in what we estimate to be around 4 million cars, or compensating owners. Every statement on it can also end up quoted in court. Saying nothing is cheaper, at least this quarter.

But Tesla can’t have it both ways. It can’t tell shareholders that unsupervised FSD is coming to customer cars by Q2 2027 while ignoring the owners who bought that exact feature years ago and whose cars will never get it. Many of them paid up to $15,000 upfront for it.

The HW3 upgrade isn’t an engineering problem at this point. Musk already said the hardware can’t do it. It’s a question of whether Tesla will pay to honor what it sold, and right now the answer looks like silence. Will an HW3 owner ever get a real plan before a judge forces one? I bet on nope.

#4829. sonnen files for insolvency in Germany as US sales double

Residential battery storage maker sonnen is reporting two very different stories today: Its German business has filed for insolvency, while sonnen USA says sales have doubled and it’s preparing to expand.

The insolvency filing comes just two months after Shell sold sonnen to investment group TIVEN. Germany’s Handelsblatt reported that sonnen GmbH confirmed the filing and informed roughly 400 employees in Wildpoldsried, Bavaria, on October 22.

For homeowners with sonnen batteries, the immediate question is what happens to service. According to Handelsblatt, the company intends to keep supporting its more than 150,000 existing customers. But a substantial overhaul is coming: Numerous subsidiaries are expected to be wound down or enter insolvency proceedings under self-administration, with only one production site remaining. The report does not identify that site.

Meanwhile, sonnen USA’s announcement describes a growing home battery business. The company says sales have doubled and production has tripled year over year, supported by expanded manufacturing in Stone Mountain, Georgia. It expects to deliver more than 180 megawatt-hours of residential battery storage in 2026.

Much of that growth comes from virtual power plants (VPPs). These connect home batteries so they can work together to support the grid, giving households another way to earn value from their solar and storage systems.

In Texas, sonnen says its SOLRITE offering serves more than 6,000 homes, combining rooftop solar, batteries, energy management, and VPP participation. In Massachusetts, its sonnenCommunity program offers cash rewards to participating homeowners in National Grid and Eversource territories. The company also reports rising sales through its Wattsmart program in Utah.

TIVEN bought the entire global business, including sonnen USA. US CEO Blake Richetta stated today that “TIVEN is firmly committed to the long-term success of sonnen USA as a strong, market-leading company in the North American VPP energy market.”

TIVEN stated that it “looks forward to bolstering the company’s impressive growth.”

But the US announcement leaves an important question unanswered: How will the German restructuring affect the US operation and its customers? It doesn’t address the insolvency filing, and sonnen USA declined to comment on developments in Germany when contacted by pv magazine.

The US growth figures show demand for sonnen’s batteries. What customers still need is a clear explanation of how manufacturing, software support, and service will be maintained through the restructuring.
